title: Understanding the Properties of Imidazolium Ionenes through Systematic Variation of Monomer Structures
abstract: Ionenes are polymers that are made up of ionic groups in the backbone. The most common ionic groups found in ionenes are quaternary ammonium groups. Imidazolium ionenes have been far less studied than ammonium ionenes and as such these ionenes will be studied. In this project, the Menshutkin reaction will be used to polymerize 1,10-dibromodecane (or similar α,ω-dihaloalkanes) with 1,4-Bis((1 H-imidaxol-1-yl)methyl)benzene (and similar derivatives) via condensation (step-growth) mechanisms. The ionene product will feature imidazolium cations in the backbone with “free” bromide (Br - ) anions which can then be exchanged to bistriflimide (Tf 2 N - ) anions to provide a means of making the ionene hydrophobic and more thermally stable. The influence of structural variables will be examined as relating to the polymer properties including solubility in various solvents, glass transition temperature, thermal stability, polymer nanostructure/organization and mechanical properties.

title: Fabrication of Porous Metal Via Free Corrosion of Hypoeutectic Compositions of Al-Cu Alloy
abstract: Nanoporous metals have recently been studied for their diverse applications in catalysis and gas separation. Often, they are made of costly metals such as gold. The present project sought to obtain a porous metal via selective dissolution of hypoeutectic aluminum-copper alloys, as the parent material. An Al-50 wt. % Cu master alloy melt was diluted with pure aluminum to create target composition ingots. These were cut into 10 x 10 x 2 mm samples, which were subsequently weighed, annealed, and fine-polished for corrosion. The corrosion in an 8% v/v NaOH solution was traced at different time intervals. Afterwards, optical microscopy allowed capturing micrographs that were studied using image analysis to measure the porosity. The corroded samples were analyzed using x-ray diffraction to verify that the selective dissolution was effective.

title: Development of Bio-Inspired Nanopatterned Surface on Polymer Thin Films for Anti-Reflective and Anti-Bacterial Coatings
abstract: Serious infectious diseases from contact with pathogenic microorganisms in our daily lives as well as the fast evolution of drug-resistant bacteria present the urgent need to develop a new functional surface that transcends antibiotics. Recently, physical methods emulating natural, bactericidal surfaces with nanopatterns have been employed in the efforts to combat bacterial adhesion by triggering mechanical rupture of the bacterial membrane. Such biomimetic nanostructures that exhibit antibacterial properties have shown promise in hard materials used for orthopedic implants such as titanium and stainless steel. Yet, little is known about the surface engineering of soft materials to attain bactericidal properties, despite numerous applications of polymers that need prevention of bacterial attachment. We aim to develop antibacterial structures on polymeric surfaces of which conventional benefits from intrinsic materials’ properties are particularly desirable. The main goal of the current study is to develop the biomimetic moth-eye structure on polymer surfaces with both antibiotic and antireflective properties. To achieve this goal, first, we will fabricate the moth-eye mimetic nanopillar-patterned structures on silicon wafers (hard molds) with differing pillar geometries and spacing. By counting colony-forming units (CFU) and live/dead cell assays of gram-negative E. coli adhered on the engineered surfaces, we will find the optimal nano-surface geometry to maximize antibacterial properties. Then, we will obtain the moth-eye mimetic structure on poly(urethane acrylate) that presents a high refractive index by the soft molding pattern transfer technique using a fluoropolymer mold with a very low surface energy. The detailed investigation on the correlation between the surface properties and the antibacterial performance will be conducted to engineer polymeric surfaces for target applications. Development of nanopatterns on polymer thin films to induce bactericidal and antireflective properties will offer a wide variety of polymer coatings for future application in monitors, phone displays, and other optical devices.

title: Hydrophobic Non-Fluorinated Polymeric Coatings on Cellulose Paper Via Initiated Chemical Vapor Deposition (iCVD)
abstract: Functional polymeric coatings present on materials serve to strengthen surface properties and enhance the versatility of said materials for applications such as packaging, flexible electronics, and microfluidics. While fluorinated polymeric coatings are commonly used for increased hydrophobicity, they can be detrimental to the environment and public health. In this work, we attempt to combat this safety issue by exploring alternative polymeric coatings that boast similar functional benefits to the surface properties of fluoropolymers using a solvent-free vacuum deposition process. Siloxane polymers were explored as an alternative to fluoropolymers, as they are common in many commercial and industrial applications and boast hydrophobicity and flexibility in coatings. Whatman cellulose chromatography papers and silicon wafers were coated with polydivinylbenzene (PDVB), poly(1,1,3,3,5,5-hexamethyl-1,5-divinyltrisiloxane) (PS5) and P(DVB- co -S5), a cross-linked polymer containing PDVB and PS5, via initiated chemical vapor deposition (iCVD). PS5 alone failed to deposit while PDVB and P(DVB- co -S5) resulted in successful coating depositions. The coatings were characterized using FTIR spectroscopy, and the hydrophobicity of the coatings were measured using contact angle goniometry. In addition, the thermal and mechanical stabilities of the coatings were demonstrated by annealing and folding samples. Consistent hydrophobicity of the coatings before and after stability tests was confirmed. Hydrophobicities used to demonstrate thermal and mechanical stabilities of PDVB and P(DVB- co -S5) were compared, with P(DVB- co -S5) coatings exhibiting the larger hydrophobicities on both cellulose papers and silicon wafers.

title: Adhesion and Shear Modulus in Block Copolymer Gels
abstract: The goal of my research is to quantify the adhesive strength of polymer gels as their molecular connectivity is decreased. Additionally, I aim to identify why such a relationship exists. Polymer gels exist throughout nature; gastropods, such as snails and slugs, produce mucus that helps them adhere to surfaces during their locomotion. Snail slime is so dilute, ranging from 91%-99% water, that it is often used as a lubricant. So, it is scientifically intriguing that it can also function as an adhesive. Thus, we have been analyzing dilute polymer organogels to determine how the decrease in connectivity increases the adhesiveness of the gel. These polymer gels are made of mineral oil and a combination of di-block and tri-block copolymers. As the composition of di-block polymer, in the gels, increases and, correspondingly tri-block copolymer decreases (since their total is held fixed), the molecular connectivity of the gel decreases. Adhesive strength was tested in shear yield-point experiments. Gels composed of 20 wt% total copolymer and 100 wt% to 40 wt% triblock copolymer (0 wt% to 60 wt% diblock copolymer) were using this experimental approach. It was determined that adhesive strength increased as the di-block composition increased while shear modulus decreased. The adhesive strength trend conflicts with that expected based upon qualitative observation. In the future, tests on a series of gels with 10 wt% total polymer composition will be conducted, as well as, alternative techniques explored to validate the observed trends.

title: Solid-Phase Extractive Polymerization As a New Method for Polyanhydride Synthesis to Limit Oxidation during Polymerization and Improve Purity for Controlled Drug Delivery
abstract: Polyanhydrides are an attractive class of erodible polymer for controlled drug delivery because they can exhibit bulk or surface erosion and they have been shown to stabilize several classes of drugs including macromolecular therapies. The traditional method of polymerizing polyanhydrides is melt polymerization where an activated acetylated diacid prepolymer is heated at 180 °C under vacuum for 1 h to 3 h. The vacuum helps to remove the condensation by-product, acetic acid, generated during polymerization. While this method is effective at producing polymers with molecular weights greater than 15 kg/mol, the intense heating can lead to thermal degradation, oxidation, and discoloration of the polymers. Another issue with this method is the quick increase in the viscosity of the melted prepolymer and growing polymer during polymerization leads to poor stirring and removal of acetic acid. To overcome the drawback of melt polycondensation we have developed a less thermally aggressive method of polymerization that we call solid-phase extractive polymerization. In this method, we use a solvent to facilitate the polycondensation while also extracting the acetic acid by-product with basic aluminum oxide. Using sebacic acid as a model diacid, we studied the effect of a solvent boiling point on the polymer molecular weight. Interestingly, we find that high boiling point solvents allow for temperatures close to that of melt polycondensation but they are not efficient at removing the acetic anhydride because the number of solvent cycles is low. Low boiling point solvents cycle many times but they do not heat the prepolymer enough to get appreciable polymerization. Methylcyclohexane and acetonitrile provide a balance in temperature and number of cycles through the basic aluminum oxide extraction media to produce polymers in the 15 kg/mol to 30 kg/mol range in 1 h. The polymers made with this method also do not exhibit significant signs of oxidation or discoloration. We believe this method may be applicable to many polymerization methods that generate a by-product.

title: Development of a Robust Procedure to Make Non-Swelling, Fast Curing Degradable, Injectable Hydrogels from Thiocure 1300 and Peg 575 Dimethacrylate
abstract: Hydrogels are an important class of biomaterials that consist of a water-swollen polymer. They can be either physically crosslinked or chemically crosslinked. Many chemically crosslinked hydrogels require UV or thermal methods to undergo crosslinking. Injectable hydrogels are hydrogels that can pass through a syringe needle into the body and therefore must either be shear thinning or undergo a reaction in a short period of time to crosslink and form a solid hydrogel once in the body. In 2009, Langer and coworkers developed a degradable injectable hydrogel from poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEG-575-DA) and ethoxylated trimethylolpropane tri-3-mercaptopropionate (ETTMP, Thiocure 1300) dissolved in phosphate-buffered saline at pH 7.5. The two components were separately passed through basic alumina before separately being cooled for 24 h in a refrigerator. Next the ETTMP and PEGDA were mixed together at 4­ °C. Curing occurred within 5 minutes. We tried to replicate this procedure but found no success in making hydrogels. In this work, we developed a robust method to cure ETTMP and PEGDA into hydrogels at pH 7.4 within 2 min. The synthesis of these hydrogel is based on using a calculated volume of precursors that results in an equimolar stoichiometric ratio of thiol and acrylate groups. We varied the height of the alumina column to determine the effect on gelation time. A range of 0.5 in. to 2.5 in. were tested in increments of 0.5 in. Gelation time decreased as the column height increased. A 2.5 in. column resulted in a 1. 33 min cure time and a 1 in. column resulted in a time of 2.3 min. We then varied the pH of phosphate-buffered saline from 7.2 to 7.6. Gelation time decreased with higher pH levels. A pH 7.2 solution cured in 3.32 min. and a pH 7.6 solution cured in 1.38 min. Based on our findings we determined the optimal parameters were a 1.5 in. column and pH 7.4 buffer. This method allows hydrogels to consistently cure in 1.5 min. We then performed a number of tests to analyze the mechanical properties of the hydrogel. Dynamic rheology was used to determine the gelation time, which was confirmed by a frequency sweep to ensure the data was within the linear viscoelastic range. Tensile testing was conducted to verify the elastic modulus of the hydrogels.

title: Optimizing the Stability and Functionalization of Imine-Linked 3D Covalent Organic Frameworks
abstract: Covalent Organic Frameworks (COFs) are a class of porous multi-dimensional polymers with well-defined molecular structures derived from their rigid starting materials. These properties give the material immense potential in applications ranging from gas storage to optoelectronics, catalysis, and water treatment. For 3D imine-linked COFs to become viable in these applications two major issues must be overcome. The first is that frameworks like COF-300 can collapse as a result of water molecules filling the pores, decreasing the overall surface area. Second, a method for simple orthogonal functionalization of the framework must also be established. Throughout our studies, we have identified two-stage synthetic conditions that preferentially generate the porous form via an amorphous intermediate state. Here we describe our work generalizing our two-stage synthetic approach and methods towards developing functionalized highly-stable 3D COFs.

title: Monitoring Temperature Induced Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) Concertation with an Applied Electric Field
abstract: Poly(N-isopropylacrylamide), or pNIPAM, is a free-radical polymerized polymer, that is commonly studied for uses in surface coatings, tissue engineering, regenerative medicine, biosensing, and more, due to its temperature responsiveness. Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS), used to measure temperature induced coacervation in determining a lower critical solution temperature (LCST), which is typically 30-35 o C for pNIPAM. We initially confirmed the LCST to be thermodynamically reversible and reproducible for both pNIPAM and an electrochemically active poly( N -isopropylacrylamide)- block -poly(ferrocenylmethyl methacrylate) block copolymer, or p(NIPAM- b -FMMA). A voltage was applied through the solution using an electrode lined cell, a technique with DLS that has not been previously reported. We created the cell by inserting copper tape to two sides of a DLS compatible cell, and the leads were connected to a voltage supply to generate an applied electric field across the light path. During the applied voltage, an increase in temperature (“ramp up”) and decreasing in temperature (“ramp down”) was used to look at hysteretic effects on the thermodynamic coacervation. Our results were similar to published values for the LCST of pNIPAM for both increasing and decreasing temperature ramps in the absence of an Applied Electric Field (AEF). However, we observed a decrease in LCST during a temperature increase in the presence in of an AEF (1 V/cm). Additionally, during the temperature decrease, the polymers remained coacervated and were no longer thermosensitive. Upon further experimentation, the same phenomenon occurred from at least 0.4 V/cm and upwards in stepwise 0.1 V/cm increments.

title: Determination of Reverse Micelle Diffusion Coefficients in Polymeric Organogels
abstract: The goal of this project is to determine diffusion coefficients for sodium bis(2-ethylhexyl) sulfosuccinate (AOT) reverse micelles through styrene-ethylene-butylene-styrene (SEBS) copolymer organogels at varying concentrations of SEBS. Characterizing the diffusivity of AOT through these gels will benefit future applications like transdermal drug delivery through informed structure-property ( i.e. , nanostructure-diffusion) relationships. Previous work in our group has shown that gel nanostructure is tuned by varying the amount of SEBS copolymer. For example, increasing the SEBS concentration increases the size of physical crosslinks and the concentration of chains occupying space in the gel, while decreasing the space between physical crosslinks. The current work uses Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) to track changes in gel AOT concentration over time for gels ranging from 10 wt% to 40 wt% SEBS. The acquired data is modeled using Fick’s laws to yield a diffusion coefficient for each gel formulation. The resultant diffusion coefficients decrease with increasing SEBS concentration. We hypothesize that the combination of aforementioned nanostructure trends are the culprit for our observed decrease in diffusion coefficient with increasing SEBS concentration. Understanding the relationship between the gel nanostructure of polymeric organogels and diffusion coefficients of these organogels will provide key insight for biomedical applications.

title: Investigating the Redox Activity and Lithiation of Boron Icosahedrons in the Solid State
abstract: In 2009, the Department of Energy established the Energy Frontier Research Center (EFRC) program to advance the scientific understanding of transformational energy storage technologies. With the support of the EFRC, the redox activity and lithiation of boron icosahedrons in the solid state was examined. These compounds consist of a 12 coordinated boron cluster decorated with a series of organic ligands. Borane clusters offer an intriguing opportunity for battery research, as organic compounds are not traditionally considered for redox activity. Borane clusters, however, exhibit three-dimensional aromaticity, resulting in delocalized electron density that allows for accessible redox activity, which is unexpected of an organic compound. With that in mind, these borane clusters can be thought of as an organic analog to the transition metals that are traditionally used in electrodes. In addition to being a unique cathode material, the organic nature of borane-based cathodes offers a high degree of redox tunability through variance of the attached functional groups during the scalable organic synthesis. The electrochemical behavior and structural dynamics of these materials was investigated through a comprehensive series of studies. Fundamental electrochemical studies under experimental conditions used in traditional battery cell design with solid film electrodes, including lithium counter electrodes and lithium hexafluorophosphate electrolyte, were conducted. Through cyclic voltammetry cycling, the properties of borane clusters that allow them to compete with traditional energy storage cells are further examined. Preliminary electrochemical cycling reveals that a derivative borane cluster decorated with lithium carboxylate exhibits redox activity at 3.4 V with a high degree of reversibility while cycling lithium. We have demonstrated the reversible (de)intercalation of Li + in borane clusters cycled in the solid state, offering a promising alternative to transition metal-based electrode materials.

title: FTIR-Based Method for Measuring Diffusion in Organogels
abstract: In the past decade, various efforts to innovate drug delivery have been developed. The diffusion of nanocarriers in hydrogels has been a common approach. This research studies the diffusion of nanocarriers in organogels, and the results can help similar studies involving both organogels or hydrogels in the future. The main objective of this research project is to develop and validate a method to characterize nanocarrier diffusion in block copolymer organogels. The main driving force of diffusion is the concentration gradient which, in this case, is the difference in the amount of the nanocarrier in the gel and the outside solution. Experiments consisted of three disk-shaped gels each containing 0-1 wt% of a selected nanocarrier. The amount of nanocarrier was measured using quantitative Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) in combination with gravimetric measurements to track gel swelling—both as a function of time. The data was then analyzed by normalizing the peak corresponding to the nanocarrier using the polymer peaks in order to see how the nanocarrier content dropped over time. After running various experiments with a wide range of polymer concentrations and two unique diffusing species, trends on how diffusion can be manipulated were established. For example, higher polymer concentration translated to a slower diffusion rate than low concentrations. Furthermore, unimer diffusion species diffused much faster than nanocarriers ( i.e. , reverse micelles). Ultimately, the proposed FTIR-based method to track diffusion of species in organogels was valid regardless of what polymer concentration or type of penetrant was used. With this information, we can help further the advancement of controlling the rate at which drugs are delivered throughout the body.

title: Analysis of Parameter Interactions with a Box-Behnken Design on the Production of Cellulose Nanocrystals through Sulfuric Acid Hydrolysis
abstract: Cellulose is a natural, abundant, and inexpensive, high-molecular-weight polymer that has attracted attention from various industrial sectors. Cellulose Nanocrystals (CNCs) are most commonly derived from acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of cellulose and are used in a variety of applications due to their remarkable mechanical, chemical, rheological, and optical properties. One barrier to mass implementation of CNCs is the high cost associated with the manufacturing process, primarily from low overall yields. Optimization of the manufacturing process offers a potential solution to increase yield, reduce cost, and enhance potential for mass production and total market approval. The goal of this study is to explore the interaction of sulfuric acid concentration (x1), hydrolysis temperature (x2), and hydrolysis time (x3) through a Box-Behnken Design (BBD) on the overall yield of CNCs through the sulfuric acid hydrolysis process. Our prior research has explored the outer limits of the practical design space and highlighted key processing parameters through a rotatable central composite design. However, our initial experimental design consisted of conditions at axial locations that were not achievable, either because of extreme conditions that completely degraded the cellulose, or at times that are unachievable (e.g. negative time). This BBD study encompasses a down-selected design space to further analyze targeted conditions for optimization of the hydrolysis process and subsequent yield. Conductometric titration was performed to analyze sulfate group density. Further, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy was carried out to investigate the extent of CNC degradation during synthesis. The parameter ranges selected for the study were 56-63 wt% (x1), 50-80 ℃ (x2), and 30-180 min (x3), with a maximum CNC yield of 73%.

title: Stability and Kinetics of Phase Transformations of Amorphous Dispersions
abstract: Many pharmaceuticals are composed of two main components: active pharmaceutical ingredients (API) and excipients. APIs are the active ingredients, while excipients are the inactive ingredients. Specifically, in pills/tablets, an API’s characteristics will greatly influence the potency or bioavailability (the ability of a compound to dissolve in the blood to be used by the body). The more bioavailable a drug is, the less is required to achieve a desired effect. Moreover, the structure has a major impact on the bioavailability. The excipient can help to control the structure of the API because whether it is amorphous, crystalline, or some intermediate can influence solubility. Generally, amorphous particles are more soluble and crystalline particles are less soluble. However, crystalline structures tend to be more stable than amorphous structures, and, consequentially, sometimes crystallize fully or partially over time. The polymer excipient helps prevent or slow down this since polymers themselves do not crystalize, so a homogeneous mixture of API and excipient would be expected to have little or no crystallization (Myerson, 2002). The Vibrating Orifice Aerosol Generator (VOAG) helps form amorphous dispersions. These dispersions comprise of a polymer excipient, polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP), and a model API (a dicarboxylic acid). These are chosen since PVP is a common excipient in many pharmaceuticals and dicarboxylic acids resemble many APIs. Solutions of various weight percents of dicarboxylic acid to PVP are dissolved in isopropanol (IPA). The VOAG works similarly to a spray dryer (commonly used in the pharmaceutical manufacturing): a solution is fed into the machine where it is sprayed, allowing individual drops to dry independently creating small particles. One main difference between the VOAG and spray dryer is that the spray dryer operates at higher temperatures, whereas the VOAG uses ambient temperatures with lower flow rates and improved droplet dispersion to allow for drying. Also, the VOAG produces a narrow droplet distribution which allows the VOAG to create particles of similar size to eliminate size dependency. We form amorphous particles and analyze their dynamic stability. Using powder x-ray diffraction (pXRD), samples are monitored regularly to determine if the particles begin to crystallize, how long this takes, and percent of API crystallization. Standards of known crystallinity are made to compare to the data to determine the percent crystallinity in the sample. This is done using partial least squares regression, peak area, and peak height. References Myerson, A. “Handbook of Industrial Crystallization.” Butterworth-Heinemann. 2002.

title: Release of N-Acetyl Cysteine from Chemically Modified Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) Hydrocephalus Catheter over Time
abstract: One of the biggest causes for hydrocephalus shunt failure is cell adhesion and eventual blockage of catheter holes. With an estimated 50% of shunts failing in the first two years of insertion in pediatric patients, decreasing cell attachment and catheter hole blockage can prolong the lifetime and effectiveness of shunts in hydrocephalic patients. From previous studies, it has been shown that treatment of the polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) surface of a standard catheter with an N-Acetyl-Cysteine layer (NAC/EDC/NHS) increases the wettability of the surface and decreases cell adhesion. Other studies show that NAC’s antioxidant behavior induces glutathione and in turn modulate cell inflammatory pathways. The current study explores the release of this NAC coating from the surface of the catheter over time. Using contact angle, nanodrop , a pressure assay, and SEM imaging, this is quantified for shunt samples incubated for 0, 10, 30, 60, and 90 days. Preliminary contact angle results show a decrease in wettability of the surface as incubation time is increased, suggesting the NAC coated surface releases the coating over time. SEM imaging has revealed a uniform coating on the surface of the catheters overtime indicating a uniform release. Nanodrop testing further verifies the discharge of the NAC coating from the catheter surfaces. This release is further confirmed with the other methods mentioned above, with in vivo experimentation ongoing. Confirming this release occurs, this creates a need for future studies on the effect of release on cell activity surrounding the shunt. Future work will consist of exploring cell activity through a pr o-inflammatory cytokin e p anel . T he effects of NAC on cell activity may transform the way hydrocephalus is treated in the future.

title: Highly Flexible and Transparent Conductor for Solar Cell
abstract: Flexible and wearable electronic technology has recently gained a significant amount of attention because of its potential applications for life improvement. Application of many existing and nouveau devices, such as electronic skin, human-machine interfaces, and health monitoring sensors, can increase comfort for better user experience. Because the most commonly used transparent conductor in photo-voltaic devices, indium tin oxide (ITO), is rigid and brittle, it cannot be used in flexible devices. Given that, as the wearable electronic and optoelectrical technology grows, the demand for a highly flexible electrode to accommodate human body movement like folding limbs or stretching muscles for such devices emerges. In this paper, a flexible electrode comprising of fused silver nanowires (AgNWs) and a conductive polymer blend having proficient conductivity and high optical transparency has been developed. The solution-processed electrode can be made at low temperature and cost, making it efficient for mass production. After multiple bending and twisting cycles, the flexible electrode film still has a sheet resistance of 24 ohm/sq. and average optical transmittance of 85%. The developed transparent electrode shows proficient flexibility and competent optoelectrical performance compared to commercial ITO, making it a promising candidate for flexible, transparent electrodes in solar cells.

title: Industrial-Applicable Method to Recycle High-Value Engineering Thermoplastics
abstract: High-value engineering plastics are increasing in demand in specialty industrial applications as well as everyday consumer items in today’s society. These materials have a high processing cost and can retain value due to its chemical stability. Just like commodity plastics, these engineering plastics face the challenges of one-time use and negative impacts on the ecosystem. For environmental and economic reasons, a method to efficiently recycle these specialized polymers would be beneficial. This research poster will describe and discuss a new method to allow these post-consumer and post-industrial engineering thermoplastics to be recycled and reprocessed with minimal changes in properties compared to the virgin polymer. Structural characterization is conducted using scanning electron microscopy as well as Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy. Static mechanical tests and hardness test will be used to measure the mechanical property changes. In the future, the same processing technology can be expanded to include other polymers that are difficult to recycle.

title: A Biomaterials Approach to Kidney Engineering: Structural and Chemical Modification of Silk Fibroin Scaffolds for in Vitro Tubulogenesis
abstract: About 14 percent of the general population suffers from chronic kidney disease (CKD). Although organ transplants and dialysis provide treatment for loss of kidney function, these are unsustainable solutions. A promising avenue lies in tissue engineering, particularly in the development of biomaterials that mimic the extracellular matrix (ECM) through the introduction of chemical markers and integration within intracellular signaling pathways. In vivo , Jagged1 (Jag1), a surface adhesion morphogen, contributes to proximal tubule cell fate and nephron patterning via Notch signaling within the ECM. However, Jagged1 shows very little activity in solution, and therefore must be bound in order to effectively signal to cells. In this work, both physical and chemical cues are introduced to silk fibroin (SF) scaffolds. A novel fabrication methodology was developed to create directionally aligned pores to promote tubule structure formation. Sponges were tested with renal proximal tubule epithelial cells (RPTECs). Compared to random pore scaffolds, the directionally aligned sponges possessed greater cell densities, with possible lumen formation occurring after two weeks in culture and two weeks under perfusion. For the binding of Jagged1, a diazonium coupling reaction was utilized to introduce sulfonic acid moieties of varying concentrations to free tyrosine residues within the directional sponges. The development of these modified tissue scaffolds for improved tubulogenesis can provide the groundwork for the development of a tissue engineered solution to chronic kidney failure.

title: Controlled Drug Release from Polymeric Coatings Fabricated Using an Electrospraying Technique
abstract: Electrospraying is an effective technique for producing polymeric coatings with smooth topographies. This technique is unique based on its ability to create reproducible coatings in ambient conditions from a plume of charged droplets. These polymeric coatings can be homogenously fabricated to incorporate potential drug molecules for delivery. The main objective of the study is to create drug loaded films that exhibit controlled released into a media, Phosphate Buffered Saline (PBS). In vivo conditions were simulated by utilizing a thermal shaker and replenishing the PBS after each model drug concentration measurement. Tailored drug release is desirable for many medical treatments, including cancer treatment. The total cumulative percentage of the model drug Rhodamine B (RhB) released over time was determined. Apart from in vivo conditions, controlled release was observed at different temperatures, by exploiting the change in the glass transition temperature ( of the polymer, Polyvinyl Acetate (PVAc). By altering the temperature, the rate at which the dropped seemed to increase. We infer that the thickness of the coating also has a role in determining the change in the . In the future we will also explore the effect of varying the coating thickness as well as the polymer on the release of RhB. We will also fabricate functionally graded coatings to produce tunable and unique release curves.

title: 3D Layer-By-Layer Electrostatic Assembly of Graphene-Noble Metal Thin Films for Electrocatalysis in PEM Fuel Cells
abstract: 3D Layer-by-Layer Electrostatic Assembly of Graphene-Noble Metal Thin Films for Electrocatalysis in PEM Fuel Cells Mark H. Jaskot, Joshua M. Musiol, Kamil Woronowicz, Pamela L. Sheehan 1 , Preston C. Haney 1 , Harry L. Moore 1 , H. Daniel Bahaghighat, Enoch A. Nagelli* Department of Chemistry & Life Science, Chemical Engineering Program United States Military Academy, West Point, NY 10996 1 Explosive Ordnance Disposal, Demilitarization & Experimental Directorate, Army Futures Command, CCDC Armaments Center, Picatinny Arsenal, NJ Abstract Graphene-metal composites offer great opportunity for cheaper and more efficient conductive materials to be applied in fuel cells. Using layer-by-layer self-assembly, graphene oxide-noble metal thin films were synthesized using electrostatic coordination between the carboxylic acid edge functional groups and platinum (Pt 2+ ) or palladium (Pd 2+ ) ions. Reduction of the films created free-standing sheets of interconnected graphene and platinum or palladium nanoparticles, held together using a poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) polymer. The films were created using platinum and palladium ions to test differences in behavior between metal ions but yielded similar results in both cases. Using UV-Vis spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, and SEM imaging, the films showed distinct presence of both graphene and the different noble metals while also displaying alignment and assembly of metal ions at the edges of each 2D graphene sheets. This 3D assembly between the noble metal nanoparticles and the graphene sheets creates the potential for these films to be used as novel nanocomposite electrodes for electrocatalysis in proton exchange membrane (PEM) fuel cells. * Contact: Dr. Enoch Nagelli , Email : enoch.nagelli@westpoint.edu

title: Hydrogel Network Characterization Using Low Field Nuclear Magnetic Resonance
abstract: Hydrogels, defined as linked polymer chains with high water content, present a growing interest as a drug delivery system. In order to optimize their use in the field, important characteristics such as mesh size and structure need to be understood. However, challenges arise when relying on the use of traditional methods such as Small Angle X-Ray Scattering (SAXS) or BET gas adsorption, which might be either inaccessible or require time-consuming sample preparation. As a result, the use of low field nuclear magnetic resonance (LF-NMR) has become an attractive alternative for hydrogel characterization. With this method, a magnetic field induces the alignment of the samples’ NMR-active nuclei, such as 1 H, followed by a radio frequency pulse which disrupts their alignment. As the magnetic field is held constant, the nuclei tend to “relax” back while the equipment collects the output signal. The relaxation time that characterizes the nuclei dephasing in the x-y axis (T 2 ) can then be used to understand the surface-solvent interactions and provide insightful information for the mesh size calculation of hydrogel samples. The present study focused on the use of LF-NMR to characterize samples made with poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA) at high (8000 Da) and low (700 Da) molecular weights using Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) pulse sequencing and CONTIN algorithm. Accuracy of LF-NMR was assessed by comparing the obtained results to SAXS results from literature for PEGDA with the same molecular weight. The same trends were observed in the mesh size calculations for both LF-NMR and SAXS, with very similar results between the two methods for similar hydrogel compositions and differences of less than three nanometers in mesh size calculations. Our results indicate that the interaction between hydrogels and water can be captured by NMR, with noticeable differences among various molecular weights and polymer concentrations. Therefore, NMR appears to be a valuable characterization method for hydrogels and similar wetted systems.

title: Morphology and Density of Organic Particles
abstract: My primary research goal is to determine the impact of initial droplet concentration and the fraction of the concentration that is small organic molecule versus polymer on the resulting particle morphology (both internal and external) with special attention paid to the particle density. It is hypothesized that a larger initial droplet concentration will lead to a particle shell earlier in the droplet evaporation process leading to a potentially hollower particle, while the particle density dependence with regards to the fraction of solids that is small molecule organic vs. polymer may be determined by the relative solubility of each molecule. Testing will be done using succinic acid as the model small organic molecule, polyvinylpyrrolidone(PVP) as the polymer of interest with methanol as the solvent. In order to accomplish these goals, a range of solutions was prepared with respect to both the initial solids concentration, as well as the relative amount of succinic acid and PVP. Thus, for this work, I focus on solution concentrations of 23.90, 47.79, and 95.58 g/L. This was done by the droplet composition of a solvent, and polymer, and a small molecule with an 11.5% limit of small molecule. I am working with succinic acid and PVP. For each of those values of total solids concentrations, I also considered a variety of fractions of succinic acid and PVP. The initial focus for these was on a range of values where the resulting particles are fully amorphous. Another focus is the internal morphology of the particles with the PVP as the polymer of interest with methanol as the solvent. In the past, researchers have used Araldite 502, DDSA, and DMP-30 to make an Araldite 502 epoxy resin for embedding, but due to the epoxy resins slightly malleable nature the particles appeared to be warped by the microtome blade, which deformed the spherical shape and internal structure of each particle. My goal is to find a more refined embedding technique which has no large change in temperature and cannot have a malleable nature. This past summer I worked with Benzil, Bisphenol-A based Bismaleimide resin, and Cashew Nut Shell Liquid as a resin to embed the particles into. I am going to further my research with the Cashew Nut Shell Liquid because of the long alkyl chains provide some flexibility because of the internal plasticization effect, which lead to a softer resin.

title: Elastomer Nanofibers Towards Wearable Electronics
abstract: Elastomers are polymers with viscoelastic properties and weak intermolecular forces that allow them to recover their original shape after being stretched. The elastomer complex that is the focus of this study is poly(2-acrylamido-2-methyl-1-propanesulfonic acid)/polyaniline/phytic acid (PAAMPSA/PANI/PA). This complex has elastic and conductive properties due to the inherent properties and electrostatic interactions of the individual components. The method used to create nanofibers is electrospinning, a production method that uses a strong electric field to draw fibers from a liquid. This provides control over the morphology of the fibers due to the parameters available for optimization (e.g., concentration of polymer in solution, applied bias, needle-to-collector distance, flow rates). An area of research that has not yet been explored is creating useful elastomer nanofibers. Blends allow the PAAMPSA/PANI/PA complex to be electrospun, made with the addition of a water-soluble polymer, poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA). Elastomer nanofibers can be used to develop new smart fabrics, biomedical sensors, electronic skin (e-skins), more efficient drug delivery, and flexible electronics.

title: Enhancement of Biocide Mitigation of Carbon Steel Biocorrosion By an Oilfield Biofilm Using a Nature-Inspired 14-Mer Anti-Biofiom Peptide
abstract: Microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC) is a threat to hydrotest, which is a critical step in confirming whether a pipeline can be commissioned. Seawater is frequently used in hydrotesting large pipelines. In this biofilm prevention study, an oilfield biofilm consortium was grown in an enriched artificial seawater followed by anaerobic incubation at 37 °C for up to 60 days. The combination of 100 ppm (w/w) 2,2-dibromo-3-nitrilopropionamide (DBNPA) + 100 nM (180 ppb) Peptide A (a biofilm dispersal agent) led to extra SRB (sulfate reducing bacteria), APB (acid producing bacteria) and GHB (general heterotrophic bacteria) sessile cell count reductions of 0.9-log, 0.8-log and 0.6-log, respectively, compared with the outcome obtained by 100 ppm DBNPA only. The cell count reductions led to enhanced mitigation of carbon steel corrosion weight loss and pitting corrosion, which were corroborated by electrochemical measurements.

title: The Influence of Relative Humidity on the Thermal Stability of Biocomposite Films
abstract: Biomaterials have been a topic of interest in material science, bioengineering, and medical fields because of its abundance in nature, environmental friendliness and compatibility in living systems. In this study, the relationship between relative humidity and the compositions of biocomposites films is explored. The introduction of water into the system leads to plasticization, or the process of changing the thermal and mechanical properties of a polymer such as thermal stability, crystallinity, and flexibility because the water molecules may interrupt intermolecular forces between the molecules present in the film. Previous research has shown that the introduction of water to such systems lowers glass transition temperature and increases the stiffness or crystallinity of the films. The biocomposites made up of Bombyx mori silk and microcrystalline cellulose were regenerated using 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium chloride and ethanol and hydrogen peroxide as coagulation agents. The thermal, mechanical, and structural properties of these films were tested using techniques that include thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The relative humidity tests were only run with DSC and conductivity because the relative humidity could be controlled under those procedures.

title: Synthesis of Temperature Responsive Polymeric Flocculants with Cationic Moieties for Environmental Remediation
abstract: Perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are a prolific and persistant contaminant in the environment, and our group is developing a novel copolymer sorbent with 2-phase LCST behavior to aid in PFAS removal. The hypothesis in question was that the incorporation of cationic comonomers will aid capture of anionic contaminants such as types of PFAS in temperature-driven polymeric flocculation. A model anionic organic dye, indigo carmine, was used as the preliminary contaminant in the pursuit of a conclusive visual remediation effect. The copolymers are primarily n-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAAm) with low levels of cationic comonomers like dimethylaminoethyl acrylate (DMAEA) or dimethylaminopropyl acrylamide (DMAPAA). The copolymers were polymerized via a free radical polymerization, and the structure and properties were characterized by NMR, GPC/SEC, FTIR, and UV-Vis spectroscopy. Comonomer was successfully incorporated as shown qualitatively in NMR spectra and an LCST shift upwards. The molecular weights were between 2 and 4 million g/mol. FTIR data was noisy and analysis did not clearly support comonomer incorporation. LCST was obtained via UV-Vis spectroscopy. The LCST of the new copolymers ranged from 33.75 to 40.2 °C, and was shown to be dependent on wavelength, unexpectedly. This result could challenge the industry norm of reporting LCST at a single wavelength of 500 nm. LCST of the poly(NIPAAm) (PNIPAAm) synthesized were between 30.5 and 33.75 °C, depending on initiator concentration. The copolymers were brought to flocculate in the presence of indigo carmine to determine if removal could visually or quantitatively be observed, but the efforts thus far have not been successful. The hypothesis cannot yet be proved or disproved as no contaminant removal has been demonstrated, but the comonomers were successfully incorporated into the copolymers and further optimizations to the organic anionic dye buffered flocculation study have been recommended.

title: Synthesis and Characterization of Pnipaam-Au@Ionp Thermo-Responsive Nanocomposites
abstract: Gold-shelled iron oxide nanoparticles (Au@IONPs) were synthesized and characterized for use in environmental remediation efforts using a variety of techniques to optimize the uniformity and tunability of the gold shell coating for the subsequent attachment of a polymeric coating using poly( N -isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAAm). A gold shell on iron oxide nanoparticles has been shown to prevent further oxidation and aggregation of the magnetic nanoparticles, while also having negligible effects on the inherent superparamagnetic properties of the IONPs. Comparisons were made between aqueous and organic media direct-coating procedures for the synthesis of the Au@IONPs. Aqueous methods employed a hot, citrate reduction of gold chloride onto the surfaces of coprecipitated IONPs. Organic methods used oleylamine for the reduction of gold chloride onto the surfaces of IONPs, synthesized by thermal decomposition, and provided added stability as a surface capping agent. DLS sizing data showed greater control over IONP aggregate sizes when using thermal decomposition methods as opposed to coprecipitation methods, and SEM/TEM images were collected of the nanoparticles. The reduction of gold chloride onto the thermally decomposed nanoparticles in organic media allowed, too, for the fine-tuning of the gold-shell thickness that was not achieved using only aqueous reduction methods. Surface-initiated, atom transfer radical polymerization (SI-ATRP) attachment of NIPAAm was then performed on each set of nanoparticles, and FTIR spectroscopy was employed to verify the successful attachment.

title: Colloidal Synthesis and Characterization of Metal Phosphide Nanoparticles for Optoelectronic Applications
abstract: Our growing energy usage, stressed by the apparent effects of climate change, has created an urgent need for sustainable sources of lighting and electricity. Successful development of such technology relies on our discovery of scalable photonic materials that can compete with current traditional group IV (Si, Ge) and III-V (GaN, GaAs) semiconductors, but have low toxicity and processing costs. Comprising of abundant, non-toxic, recyclable elements, nanoscale metal phosphide systems have garnered interest for such applications. To date, however, development of nanoscale metal phosphides has been deterred because of issues like the toxicity of metal and phosphorus precursors, poor stability under atmospheric conditions, and low quantum yield. In this work, we present reliable colloidal routes to group II and group IV phosphide (II – Zn, IV – Sn, Ge) nanocrystals from various metal and phosphorus precursors, some environmentally benign. We present optimization of synthesis protocols to allow for tunability of nanocrystal size and size dispersity. Structure and optoelectronic property relationships are explored via x-ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and x-ray absorption spectroscopy. Finally, we show preliminary results on implementation of these materials in functional devices.

title: Rate Measurement and Extraction for Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence Materials
abstract: In recent years, an increasing amount of researches has been focusing on organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs), which have unprecedented advancements in display and lighting technologies. Organic electronic materials generate lights through a process called electroluminescence in which singlet and triplet excitons are formed in the first step. Singlet excitons relax to ground state and produce light while the triplet excitons dissipate their energies to the surroundings as heat. Several strategies such as thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) have been proposed to convert up to 100% of the excitons in the device into the light. In this study, a type of TADF material, 4Cz-IPN is used to demonstrate the delay fluorescence property. A combination of optical, electronic and cooling systems is built to study the temperature dependence of TADF materials and to extract the rates in the TADF process. These rates can be used to calculate the energy gap between triplet and singlet excited states, and thus giving guidance of TADF material design. This system can be applied to various topics such as the influence of gold particles doped in the TADF materials, and the host-dependence of TADF materials.

title: Photonic Crystals Sensors Enabled By Peroxide-Responsive Shape Memory Polymers
abstract: Here we report novel chromogenic sensors that exhibit a change of color when exposed to an external stimulus, such as heat, pressure, shear stress, acoustic waves, and exposure to various liquids or gases. By fabricating shape memory polymers (SMPs) into the structure known as a photonics crystal, we have developed SMP sensors with dual-shape capabilities. Such sensors work by changing its shape from a predetermined shape to its permanent photonic crystal shape when exposed to the appropriate stimulus. Having potential applications ranging from user-friendly environmental monitoring to specifically detecting chemicals, these sensors introduce a more efficient alternative because they are easily perceived, inexpensive, reusable, have a small footprint, and are time and energy efficient. The active components of the SMP sensors are a few μm thick macroporous photonic crystal layers, which are fabricated using self-assembled, 3-D highly ordered colloidal crystals as structural templates. This microscopic thin-film configuration renders orders of magnitude faster response speed than bulky SMP samples in traditional applications. Moreover, by leveraging easily perceived color changes, which is associated with the unconventional all-room-temperature shape memory cycles enabled by the recent discovery of a new series of multi-stimuli-responsive SMPs, detection of certain analyte in complex solutions, such as hydrogen peroxide in commercial products, has been demonstrated with a detection limit as low as 1%.

title: Optical Characterization and Purification of DNA-Wrapped Single-Wall Carbon Nanotubes at Controlled pH
abstract: Single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) have unique optical, electronic, and chemical properties which can be utilized for an extensive range of potential applications, including biosensing and bioimaging. The DNA wrapping of SWCNTs has been proven an efficient method for dispersing nanotubes in an aqueous medium and their subsequent purification of chirality-defined SWCNTs. By inducing DNA conformational changes on the sidewall of SWCNTs through precise control of solvent pH, stable hybrids of DNA-wrapped SWCNTs (DNA-SWCNTs) with increased photoluminescence can be obtained. In this work, we monitored the effect of pH on optical properties of DNA-SWCNTs using single-stranded DNA of (GT) n sequences with n = 6, 10, 15, 20 at a broad range of pH 1-13. It was hypothesized that the site-specific deprotonation of nucleotide bases in basic regime at pH ≈ 12 promotes hydrogen bonding between the bases in (GT) n DNA; therefore, causing conformational changes in DNA coating structures. This conformational change led to increased fluorescence emission of nanotubes up to 7 times by effectively shielding quenching species in solvent from the surface of SWCNTs. In addition, the effect of nanotube concentration and excess unbound DNA on optical properties of DNA-SWCNTs were explored. The phenomenon of a pH-induced conformational change of DNA on nanotubes was further explored for SWCNT purification using a polymer aqueous two-phase separation method. Our preliminary work showed the potential of separating single-chirality SWCNTs by precise control of pH using specific DNA sequences. Future work will focus on developing a scalable method for separating chirality-defined SWCNTs, that can be utilized for biological sensing and imaging applications.

title: Vapor Induced Phase Transition of Cesium Lead Halide Perovskite Thin Films for Novel Use in Solar Cells
abstract: In recent years, perovskite solar cells have emerged as a promising new alternative to the current silicon-based panels which have dominated the market. Research was done to characterize the black to clear phase transition undergone by thin films of cesium lead halide perovskite when exposed to various solvent vapors. The thin films of a cesium lead halide perovskite were exposed to a constant partial pressure of different solvent vapors, and the kinetics of the transition from the perovskite phase to the non-perovskite δ-phase were tracked by absorption spectroscopy. We find that other common solvents, in addition to the previously known water and alcohols (MeOH and EtOH), will catalyze this phase transition. Interestingly, we find sigmoidal kinetics for this process, indicating a cooperative nature whereby the transition of one domain further catalyzes the subsequent transition of other domains. Furthermore, we find that the rate of the phase change appears to be affected but not wholly governed by molecular dipole strength. This foundational work yields deepened understanding of the mechanisms of the clear to black phase transition in halide perovskites. In future, perovskite solar cells could be designed to resist undergoing this phase transition, so that they remain black and photovoltaically active, or they could potentially be designed to exploit this transition in a product such as a dynamically switching photovoltaic window.

title: PET Can be a Sustainable Option for Replacing Polyols in the Production Process of Polyurethane Foams
abstract: Nowadays there is a constant increase in the consumption of plastic worldwide, its growth rate is about 6% every year, which is causing plastic residues end up into water sources and ecosystems. The main polymer found as residue is PET since it is widely used as a packing material in food industry. One way to mitigate this waste is through recycling, some companies try to develop new uses for this polymer. One of the industries interested in its use are companies manufacturing rigid polyurethane foams. A polyurethane foam is a material with a high thermic performance, useful for maintaining a constant temperature inside industrial equipment and reducing energy consumption; it is also impermeable and due to its capacity of creating a sealing layer it can avoid air and water leaks. These foams are produced from a reaction between polyol and an isocyanate.

title: Multimaterial Aerosol Jet Printing of Functionally Graded Nanocomposites
abstract: Advanced Materials Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM, USA Aerosol jet printing offers a digital, non-contact, high-resolution direct-write capability with broad materials compatibility. In this work, a multimaterial aerosol jet printhead is designed for in-line mixing of multiple functional inks. Drawing on fluid dynamics modeling and 3D printing for custom printhead design, this enables direct patterning of compositionally-graded films. In this case, COMSOL modeling supports static mixer development tuned for relevant aerosol parameters, with geometry optimization based on mixing efficacy, mixer volume, and particle transfer efficiency. A proof-of-concept experiment using a fluorescent tracer in epoxy and acrylate matrixes validates this approach and allows straightforward visualization and characterization. In this case, composition information is obtained from fluorescence microscopy and profilometry measurements to calibrate deposition parameters and assess print quality. This materials system is then extended to incorporate ZrO 2 nanoparticles to tailor optical and dielectric properties. Overall, this multimaterial aerosol jet printing method provides a rapid, digital, and low-waste method to control print composition on the fly, establishing this nascent technology as a compelling platform for diverse applications including, but not limited to, functionally-graded electronic, optical, and magnetic materials. title: Design and Application of High-Performance Ionene Composites
abstract: Media for state-of-the-art gas separation membranes draws from material classes including ionic liquids (ILs), poly(ILs), and supported liquid membranes (SLMs) as well as more robust materials including polymers with varied functionality. Ionenes are polymers which contain ionic moieties along the main chain, rather than as pendants, which can be designed to harness the advantageous properties and structural elements typically associated with high-performance (HP) engineering polymers (i.e. aromatic character, imide or amide linkages). We have recently investigated the design, synthesis, and application of a new class of HP ionenes, which incorporate imidazolium cations (paired with Tf 2 N anions) along the main chain, alternating with diverse functional groups. The modular design of functional bis(imidazoles) and bulky dihalide monomers linked via the Menshutkin reaction, we have synthesized numerous derivatives of these ionenes which can be processed and tuned for a variety of applications. These materials exhibit intriguing self-assembly and nanostructuring, which is dictated by the complex combination of ionic and functional intermolecular interactions, leading to sophisticated materials with good thermal and mechanical stability. This structuring can be further tailored via the addition of “free” imidazolium-based ILs or functional ionic fillers, which serve as a non-covalent crosslink between polymer chains, stabilizing the polymer matrix and increasing the free volume between chains. These composites are processed into thin films (solvent-cast or melt-pressed) and the performance of these materials as membranes for light gas separations is analyzed. Due to the diverse potential structural combinations which lead to unique properties and behaviors, certain derivatives have also been investigated as functional coatings, elastomeric shape memory materials, additives, and fibers for additive manufacturing. Here, we present the development of these ionene composites resulting from complex monomer units, and the impact of design and processing on structure-property relationships and performance in the aforementioned applications.

title: Efficient Removal of Microcystin-LR Cyanobacterial Toxins from Contaminated Freshwater By Biocompatible Polymer Coacervates
abstract: Microcystin-LR (MC-LR) is one of many toxins released upon the lysis of cyanobacteria, blue-green algae, and some cells in Great Lakes and other natural freshwater sources, which imposes potential health risk to humans and animals. The safe level of MC-LR in drinking water according to the World and Health Organization (WHO) is 1μg/L, yet its concentration in natural freshwater could reach to 0.2-1800μg/L when cyanobacteria bloom in the summer, making perilous for consumption and daily uses. In this research, we explore a new polymer flocculate based on the coacervate complexation of biocompatible polyethylene oxide (PEO) and polyacrylic acid (PAA) via hydrogen bonding to demonstrate efficient coacervate removal of MC-LR from aqueous solutions. Gel-like PEO-PAA complexes are added to model contaminated water of varied concentration from 1-5000 μg/L; the supernatant aqueous phase is separated from the polymer coacervate complex after mixing for 5-30 min and the residual MC-LR concentration in aqueous solution is quantified by UV-vis spectroscopy and mass spectroscopy. Preliminary results show that our coacervate flocculates could remove up to 95% of MC-LR with an initial concentration of 1000μg/L. The efficiency of coacervated complexes at varied MC-LR concentration and PEO-to-PAA molar ratios are under current investigation, seeking an optimal PEO-to-PAA composition ratio for maximal efficiency of MC-LR removal.

title: Nanocomposite Based Tough Hydrogels for Fabrication of ECG Monitoring Device
abstract: Hydrogel is a three-dimensional (3D) network of hydrophilic polymers that can hold a lot of water while keeping up the structure because of concoction or physical cross-connecting of individual polymer chains. By definition, water must establish at rate 10% of the all-over weight (or volume) for a material to be a hydrogel. It likewise has a level of adaptability fundamentally the same as regular tissue because of their huge water content. They are delicate material that carries on like skin. Intense hydrogels are delicate however have high perseverance to strain with satisfactory versatility. Hydrogels with directing properties and sturdiness are broadly utilized in numerous sensor gadgets that can be utilized in biotechnology and biomedical applications. In our work we have synthesized a polymer-Ag nanocomposite based ionic and conductive hydrogel to utilize it as a sensor material. These hydrogels are intense enough to oppose cut by a knife with 900% stretch capacity. The conductive hydrogels were utilized to create ECG sensor. Arduino based code was additionally used to build up an easy to use application for continuous ECG monitoring and information securing. Along these lines, the hydrogel sensors are promising competitor in numerous medical gadgets and other biomedical application.

title: Development and Characterization of Bio-Based Thermosets from Birch Bark
abstract: Pollution from plastic waste is a growing global issue. Traditional petroleum-derived plastics can take hundreds of years to degrade naturally and petroleum stores are quickly depleting. As such, bio-based plastics are increasing in popularity in both scientific and consumer spheres as they offer a sustainable alternative to petroleum-based plastics. In this work, we investigate the use of betulin, a naturally-occurring diol that can be extracted from birch bark in high yields, as a building block for the formation of bio-based polyester thermosets. We systematically assess the choice of co-monomers on the thermomechanical and degradative properties of the resulting polymers. Our results show that the room temperature moduli range from 2.0 to 790 MPa and the glass transition temperatures are tunable over a 100°C range depending upon the co-monomer selected. Moreover, all samples exhibit thermal stability above 300°C in both nitrogen and air. This work is part of a larger study focused on the valorization of betulin for commodity plastics. The results presented here demonstrate that betulin is a promising building block for the design of bio-based thermosets.

title: Synthesis of Polymeric Membranes with Carboxylic Acid and Thiol Groups for Ion Adsorption Applications
abstract: The removal of heavy-metal ions from industrial wastewater is highly important due to their health and environmental effects. Additionally, the recent increase in the usage of electronic devices has led to an increased usage of lanthanides, which should be recycled due to their high value. Adsorption and ion exchange technologies have been used for these applications and further development of sustainable technology in these areas is crucial. This work involves the characterization, fabrication, and performance testing of polymeric membranes containing carboxylic acid and thiol groups, which are suitable for these applications. Membrane fabrication began with the polymerization of polyacrylic acid (PAA) in the pores of commercial polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes to add carboxylic acid groups that can form complexes with cations, such as La 3+ . Furthermore, membranes containing thiol groups, which have a strong affinity for heavy metal ions, were fabricated by covalently attaching cysteamine to PAA. The incorporation of PAA into a PVDF membrane was verified by a change in surface charge of the modified membrane near the pK a of PAA (~4-5). 3.7 g La 3+ /m 2 membrane was captured by a PVDF-PAA membrane via convective-flow ion exchange. The binding of cysteamine to PVDF-PAA membranes was confirmed by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy, which indicated the presence of adsorbed silver in the membrane pores. When treating a feed containing 40 - 50 ppb of Hg 2+ and 70 ppm of Ca 2+ , a thiol-functionalized membrane captured 82% of the Hg 2+ in one pass. The capture of La 3+ by a PVDF-PAA membrane and Hg 2+ by a cysteamine-functionalized PVDF-PAA membrane demonstrated the versatility of the PVDF-PAA membrane as a base for multiple applications involving the capture of metal ions. Dr. Evan Hatakeyama of Chevron Energy Technology Company provided guidance on this research. This research was supported by Chevron Energy Technology Company, NSF EPSCoR, and NIEHS-SRP.

title: CFD and PBM Modeling of Particle Aggregation in Mixing Tanks
abstract: Latex emulsions are systems containing a discrete phase of latex particles dispersed in a continuous aqueous phase and are widely used in industrial mixing processes. In the mixing of latex emulsions, small particles aggregate into larger, more uniform particles to establish a particle size distribution (PSD) required for quality standards. Particle aggregation and colloidal interactions are governed by the Derjaguin, Landau, Verwey, Overbeek (DLVO) theory. Perikinetic aggregation due to Brownian motion is the dominant form of aggregation for very small particles in latex emulsions. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Population Balance Modeling (PBM) are two techniques that are used to develop simulations and computational models of the mixing and particle aggregation involved in emulsion mixing processes. CFD is used to model the fluid and flow properties associated with the mixing, whereas PBM uses population balance equations to track the PSD of the latex particles. This project aims to understand the complexities associated with colloidal dispersions and emulsion aggregation in mixing tanks and the issues involved with scaling-up these mixing processes. By examining (1) the velocity profiles, (2) the change of PSD over time, and (3) the specific areas of the tank at which particles accumulate, two tanks of different sizes can be compared. Using ANSYS Fluent, CFD-PBM simulations of latex particle aggregation in water were run in a Pilot Plant tank and a larger Manufacturing tank using a user-defined function based in DLVO theory to calculate particle aggregation rates. The simulations illustrate a lack of mixing in areas at the top and near the wall of the tank in addition to slower and less uniform particle aggregation patterns in the Manufacturing tank compared to the Pilot Plant tank.

title: Elucidating Structure-Property Relationships of Atomically-Precise Gold Nanoclusters from Density Functional Theory
abstract: In recent years, ligand-protected Au nanoclusters (NCs) have retained tremendous interest due to their structural determination with atomic precision, unique optical and electronic properties, and great potential in diverse nanotechnological applications like catalysis, biomedicine and imaging. Since their discovery, Density Functional Theory (DFT) has been instrumental in calculating the electronic properties of NCs. Although accurate, DFT is computationally expensive, especially for NC systems consisting of a couple of hundred atoms. Thus, rapid methods that retain the accuracy of DFT are highly sought after to screen NCs exhibiting desirable electronic properties. Towards this goal, we developed a computational framework to discover structure-property relationships on ligand-protected Au NCs. Our approach connects NC descriptors based solely on experimental structural data to electronic properties calculated with DFT. Applying our framework, we developed a universal NC electronic gap model based on a sample of 22 NCs ranging from 18 to 102 Au atoms with 8 different ligand types. The model was in turn used to elucidate the structural features that dictate electronic gaps of NCs. Overall, this research accelerates materials discovery at the nanoscale by developing structure activity relationships on ligand protected NCs. These relationships elucidate how NC size (number of Au atoms) and presence of ligands (number of thiol ligands) affect the NC electronic properties and are able to identify specific NC morphologies that exhibit desired electronic properties.

title: Evaluating and Modeling the Strength of 3D Printed Samples Using a Design of Experiments Framework
abstract: Advanced technologies that precisely and rapidly convert designs into real-world products have the potential to transform industries ranging from healthcare to aerospace. Additive manufacturing offers advantages over subtractive manufacturing methods, which include such advantages as high accuracy prototyping, complex internal geometries, and less material waste. In particular, stereolithography (SLA) printing offers a reliable platform for generating mechanically isotropic parts with high feature resolution. In SLA printing, photo-sensitive liquid resin is selectively cured using UV light into solid parts in a layer-by-layer process based on specifications from a computer-aided design stereolithography file (STL). Potential challenges associated with large-scale use of SLA printing are the need for significant quantities of specialized liquid resins and long printing times. In this work, we designed and tested part geometries with varied void patterns and fractions to investigate the trade-off between reduced material use and decreased mechanical strength. To determine which patterns are most effective at maintaining the material strength per weight, we investigated three different void patterns with varying void fractions at two layer heights using a statistical design of experiments (DOE) methodology. The parts were designed and tested in accordance with ASTM standards and post-cured in a custom-built curing chamber. Tensile tests were used to measure the Young’s modulus and ultimate tensile strength for each part using an Instron testing system. Overall, circular void patterns resulted in the highest mechanical strength for a given void fraction. Moreover, finite element analysis was utilized to inform and corroborate the experimental results. This work can inform the design of parts with decreased material use, making the process more economical.

title: Optimizing the Alignment of Electrospun Pnipam:PLGA Blendednanofibers for Cell Sheet Engineering
abstract: Cell sheet engineering has emerged as a new tissue engineering strategy to harvest cells with their deposited extracellular matrix (ECM) as intact sheets. To prevent disrupting their ECM, thermoresponsive culture dishes are utilized for harvesting cells instead of using enzymatic treatment. One such thermoresponsive polymer that has been used for the culture of cell sheets is poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM), which exhibits a reversible phase change at its lower critical solution temperature (LCST) of 32°C. At an incubation temperature of 37°C, PNIPAM exhibits a hydrophobic state, allowing for cells to adhere and proliferate. Various tissues in the human body, such as vascular smooth muscle cells (SMCs), tendons, bones and skeletal muscles, rely on cellular alignment for proper function; therefore, it is favorable to engineer aligned cell sheets for successful transplantation. In order to culture aligned cell sheets, nanofibers can be used as a 3D scaffold for cell growth and proliferation. Electrospinning is a promising technique for fabricating scaffolds due to its ability to easily and inexpensively manipulate nanofiber morphology. In this study, we optimized the electrospinning process for PNIPAM, PLGA, and PNIPAM:PLGA blended nanofibers using a statistical design of experiment of key process parameters. Through extensive experimental testing and statistical DOE, we were able to achieve an alignment coherency of over 80% for PLGA, PNIPAM, and blended fibers. Results showed that reducing polymer solution concentration resulted in fibers with smaller diameters and increasing the speed of the mandrel increased nanofiber alignment. Future work will assess material thermal responsiveness by measuring cellular attachment and release.

title: Flow-Induced Crystallization of Fatty Acid Methyl Esters
abstract: Determining effects of concentration and shear-flow on the crystallization temperature of pure Fatty Acid Methyl Esters (FAMEs) and binary mixtures of FAMEs could lead to methods of altering cloud point of biodiesel fuels. The widespread implementation of biodiesel fuels is hindered partially by the cloud point of their FAMEs while in fuel or pipelines. Three FAMEs were studied, methyl myristate, methyl palmitate, and methyl stearate; pure and binary mixtures were prepared at 0/100, 20/80, 40/60, 60/40, 80/20 and 100/0 weight percent. Crystallization temperatures were observed as part of a phase study for the pure and binary FAME mixtures under static conditions. Then, rheology studies were conducted to determine the flow-induced crystallization temperature. The hypothesis of the project was that increasing shear rate increases crystallization temperature. Binary mixtures have shown to reduce the crystallization temperature from that of the pure components under static conditions and were expected to show even lower crystallization temperatures under flow. Crystallization temperature under flow has not consistently depressed, rather it has followed the trend taken by the highest concentration FAME.

title: Cyclic Voltammetric and Spectroelectrochemical Characterization of Polymer Thin Films
abstract: Electrochemistry is a well established field in analytical chemistry. One property of great interest in electrochemistry is the apparent charge transfer diffusion coefficient of polymer thin films. Combining electrochemical techniques with spectroscopy, new insights can be gained on the characteristics of the polymer film. Cyclic voltammetry was used to prepare polymer films of tris(5-amino-1,10-phenanthroline)ruthenium(II) and iron(II) on Indium Tin Oxide (ITO) surfaces. When the film was electrochemically reduced, a visible color change was measured spectroscopically and related to the charge transfer rate. A correlation was studied between the spectrochemical, electrochemical and impedance measurements. While under diffusion controlled conditions, this correlation was used to find the apparent charge transfer diffusion coefficient. This coefficient is useful for applications in other research and provides a better understanding of polymer thin films.

title: Measuring the Surface Tension of Different Surfactants to Make Better Polyhipes
abstract: Foams and emulsions are created by the combination of either two immiscible liquids or one liquid and a gas with the addition of a surfactant. Water and a hydrophobic phase, such as a monomer, are two liquids that are commonly used. As the water and monomer do not mix, a surfactant must be used. A surfactant is a molecule with hydrophilic and hydrophobic components, which allows the two immiscible materials to mix. The first step in creating a polymer foam is creating an emulsion that consists of the monomer (continuous phase), water (dispersed phase), and a surfactant. Then the emulsion is polymerized resulting in a polymer foam filled with water. These voids are often interconnected in the polymer, so liquid is able to flow in and out. The water is then dried out of the foam to result in a polymer foam with voids. These polymer foams have been proven useful in many engineering applications such as tissue engineering, cosmetics, and food science. The goal when making these emulsions is to increase the surface area of the voids in the polymer foam to enable more interaction between the surfactant and the fluid. This is a result of many smaller voids being distributed throughout the foam rather than larger voids existing in a smaller quantity. The way void size is controlled is through the manipulation of surface tension. Surface tension is a resistance force that exists on the surface of a liquid. It is important for the creation of emulsions because the lower the surface tension, the higher the emulsion surface area. After testing the surface tensions of different surfactants with other monomers, a relationship between surface tension and concentration can be quantified. As more surfactant is added, the surface tension will decrease with the goal of determining the lowest possible surface tension that can be achieved. The concentration at which this occurs is called the critical micelle concentration. As a result of how low the CMC found is, it can be determined which surfactants work best with different mixtures and better emulsions can be achieved. Using a tensiometer, concentrations of the surfactants Triton X-100, C-TAB, Kaolin, Span 80, SDS, and Hypromellose in the monomers Styrene and 2-Ethylhexyl acrylate were evaluated.
