title: Architected Porous Media for Metered Liquid Transfer Flexographic Printing
abstract: The development of printed and unconventional electronic devices to meet application-specific needs requires innovation in printing technologies. Flexography (flexo), a rubber-stamping method developed in the 19th century, has proven scalable (meters per second) for graphic arts but is underdeveloped for printed electronics, particularly transistor and transparent electrode applications, due to limited feature resolution (>50 µm). Although much work has gone into understanding the structural and fluid mechanics of the ink transfer processes, little attention has been paid to the actual stamp, typically fabricated via polymer replication of a hard master. The elastomeric stamp is top-side inked and compressed on a substrate, a process that has inherent limits for materials transfer and results in uneven pixel quality (poor feature resolution) due to compression-induced spreading. However, consider a porous stamp that undergoes precise deformation such as negative Poisson’s ratio (NPR) during this process. Here, ink transfer could be a metered process with the pore-space being the reservoir and the mechanical deformation being the “metering pump”. Moreover, a stamp that exhibits a slight NPR may allow for controlled expulsion and sharper transfer foot print (minimal line-edge roughness). Only recently has it been feasible to produce such engineered structures at high resolution, for example, using multiphoton-induced, direct laser writing (DLW). Here we investigate how precisely architected (e.g., NPR and a structured pore size distribution), 3D porous media can control the fluid saturation/capillary pressure characteristics upon mechanical compression to enable high fidelity/metered material transfer for high speed printing. In this study, we systematically investigate the effects of porosity, pore size distribution and microstructure compression on flexographic ink transfer using iterative arrays of high-resolution (<1 µm feature size) DLW structures to converge on optimized forms. Fluid dynamics simulations of defined poroelastic media provide further insight into metering ink transfer during compression. Overall, this work illustrates the design flexibility and precision control of micro- features/fluid dynamics enabled using form-fabrication of flexographic forms.

title: An Assessment of the Biofilm-Prevention Efficacy of a Silver Carboxylate Eluting Titanium Dioxide and Polydimethylsiloxane Matrix on Spinal Implants
abstract: Healthcare acquired infections (HAI) cause an increased burden and excess length of hospital stays (LOS), which accounts for approximately 90% of total costs. 1 Moreover, infection rates in biomedical implants can be as high as 4% for some devices and can cause up to $50,000 to fix. 2 These infections specifically may involve the spread of a family of gram-negative bacteria, Enterobacteriaceae (CPE), including Serratia marcescens , and is becoming a global public health problem associated with healthcare facilities. 3 Human infections by this pathogen were not recognized until the latter half of the 20th century. 4 S. marcescens is a gram-negative bacterium commonly associated with chronic orthopedic wounds, specifically in the spine. These infections may be comprised of biofilms, which are communities of microorganisms that are attached to a surface and are resistant to antibiotics, resulting in recurrent Surgical Site Infections (SSIs). 5 However, in recent years the use of silver as an antimicrobial agent has received attention for its ability to combat biofilm formation through its long-lasting release, broad antibacterial spectrum, and low incidence of antibiotic resistance. 6 In response to these concerns, we have developed a coating composed of a titanium dioxide and polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) matrix doped with silver carboxylate that allows for the controlled release of silver, acting as an antibiotic-independent antimicrobial by preventing biofilm formation. This project involved the assessment of the antimicrobial capabilities of various composition ratios of the matrix and silver carboxylate on three spinal implant materials. Stainless steel, titanium, and polyetheretherketone (PEEK) were chosen for this study due to their varying topographies, but also widespread use and effectiveness as surgical implants. The coating does not affect the mean roughness of the implant and does not interfere with osseointegration. The layering is thin, on the order of 10-100 nm, and can be applied incrementally to create a desired thickness. Multiple trials showed that microbial adherence and percent area coverage decreased with increasing silver dosage. Across all implants, the best performance was found using a 95% TiO 2 and 5% PDMS matrix, with a 10x concentration of silver carboxylate. Scanning electron microscopy and confocal microscopy analysis showed the highest CFU per area for the stainless steel, resulting in a higher adherence rate for S. marcescens on stainless steel than the other two materials. Future direction of this study will constitute of an in-depth characterization and improvement of the coating itself.

title: Synthesis and Characterization of Multifunctional Bio-Based Polybenzoxazines and Their Blends with Epoxy Resins
abstract: Synthesis and Characterization of Multifunctional Bio-Based Polybenzoxazines and their Blends with Epoxy Resins Sarah Salazar, Amanda McCahill, Alexandra Chong, Joseph F. Stanzione III Department of Chemical Engineering, Rowan University, Glassboro, NJ 08028 Abstract The uncertainty of the petroleum industry and increase in environmental concerns has caused a growing interest in bio-based polymers. Polybenzoxazines are polymers that possess high glass transition temperatures, high char yields, good mechanical properties, and low shrinkage upon curing. In addition, the structures of benzoxazines allow for remarkable molecular design flexibility and can be used in numerous applications, such as lightweight aviation composite parts. Bio-based chemicals have the potential to replace petroleum-based benzoxazine platform molecules such as BPA, which has displayed toxic effects on human health and the environment. Additionally, benzoxazines are known to produce brittle polymers with low crosslink densities, so blending with epoxy resins have shown to improve crosslink densities resulting in better mechanical properties of the polymers. Higher degrees of oxazine functionality have shown to display better mechanical and thermal properties of polybenzoxazines. Bio-based mono-, di-, and tri-functional benzoxazines were synthesized and characterized based on varying degrees of functionality. The benzoxazines with each targeted oxazine functionality were synthesized via Mannich condensations involving guaiacol and vanillin combined with furfurylamine and paraformaldehyde. Monofunctional benzoxazines were blended with different weight percents of diglycidyl ether of bisphenol A (DGEBA) and subsequently cured. These uncured and cured resin mixtures were characterized using DSC, TGA and DMA to understand their structure-property relationships. Overall, bio-based benzoxazines with increased oxazine functionality and their epoxy blends were investigated to produce environmentally sustainable polymers with enhanced thermal and mechanical properties.

title: Confined Diffusion through Macroporous Structures
abstract: Currently, confined mass transport through subsurface environments (e.g., soil, sediment, rock) is primarily investigated using computer simulations or run-off studies of core samples. Computer simulations lack empirical grounding while core studies provide little insight into the solutes’ interactions with the internal structure. We created an empirical model of these complex subsurface systems that observed individual particle trajectories. Macroporous structures (possessing a pore size greater than 50 nm) were created from silica (< 10 µm) packed on Piranha cleaned glass wafers and inside cured polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) flow channels. We employed single-particle tracking methods to visualize the path of 40 nm carboxylate-modified fluorospheres through macroporous structures. A Nikon A1R microscope capable of Laser Scanning Confocal and Total Internal Reflectance Fluorescence (TIRF) with an attached camera was used. Two kinds of tracking experiments were conducted: static diffusion and flow. During experimental runs, the capture images were acquired at a rate of 50 ms and combined in a single movie (2400 frames per movie). The movies were analyzed using in-house single-particle tracking code. Trajectory maps, tortuosity averages and diffusion coefficients were calculated for each sample. Analyzing the static diffusion experiments, tracer particles in 4.3 μm structure experienced more tortuous paths compared to the 4.3 μm + 9.2 μm and 9.2 μm structures. All packing structures yielded lower diffusion coefficients compared to unconfined diffusion. The flow experiments posed a challenge in creating a close packed porous structure that remained immobile but still allowed fluid flow. Future work will observe flow behavior through packed structures and derive mathematical relationships. The overall goal of this project is to inform mass transport through low porosity environments such as soil systems and porous rock.

title: Fabrication of Microporous Hyaluronic Acid Hydrogels through Salt Leaching
abstract: Water-absorbing polymeric constructs, such as hydrogels, have been increasingly utilized for tissue engineering purposes, as well as in vitro models to study disease. Specifically, hyaluronic acid (HA)-based hydrogels have been extensively utilized, as HA is a major component of the extracellular matrix. Herein, we report a simple procedure on the incorporation of a microporous structure within an HA hydrogel. By utilizing methacrylated hyaluronic acid, dithiothreitol (DTT) as a crosslinker, and implementing salt particles of various diameters to act as porogens, a microporous structure was obtained through a salt leaching technique. Scanning electron microscopy, rheological testing, and swelling studies were carried out to analyze the microporous HA hydrogels. It was found that an increase in salt particle diameter resulted in microporous hydrogels with increased overall pore areas that were all significantly different from control hydrogels. The microporous hydrogels were also found to be able to retain significantly larger quantities of water than control hydrogels; however, the microporous hydrogels exhibited significantly lower storage moduli than control hydrogels. Additional studies to determine cell viability and degradation behavior using the hyaluronidase enzyme are currently being carried out to further characterize the hydrogels. Such a system could provide a useful tool for studying cell-matrix interactions in vitro in a physiologically relevant setting.

title: Colloidal Gelation of Silica Suspensions with Varying Salt and Surfactant Concentrations
abstract: Colloidal gelation can be useful to prevent sedimentation of complex fluid products such as oral medicines or paints. Colloidal particles remain suspended in a liquid when interparticle repulsive forces are stronger than the attractive forces, especially at low volume fractions. When attractive forces dominate, colloidal particles may form an “attractive gel”. For aqueous suspensions of charged colloidal particles, electrostatic repulsive forces can be weakened by counterions. Similarly, agents can be added to strengthen attractive forces. For ionic surfactants at concentrations below the critical micelle concentration (CMC), there are no micelles, and they act as simple electrolytes. It is hypothesized that above the CMC of sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) surfactants (CMC = 8 mM), micelles will introduce attractive depletion forces between particles, altering gelation. Consequently, when compared to the baseline system of a simple salt, one may expect colloidal suspensions to gel at lower concentrations of SDS than of NaCl. Using negatively charged silica in water as a model colloidal system, the goal is to understand how gelation phase behavior differs in the presence of increasing concentrations of simple NaCl electrolyte versus SDS. The phase behavior of Ludox colloidal silica was characterized according to transitions from a fluid to an attractive gel phase. Purified suspensions were prepared at a variety of silica concentrations. Suspensions were monitored over time to record the onset gelation time, which was characterized qualitatively based on flow characteristics of the sample. Thus far, a phase diagram mapping the effects of added salt and SDS on the silica suspensions has been prepared. The phase boundary between gel and fluid phases for SDS samples was observed at two to four times higher concentrations as compared to the phase boundary for NaCl samples for all the silica concentrations studied. In addition, gelation was faster for samples containing NaCl as compared to those containing equivalent concentrations of SDS. Whereas all NaCl added to solution contributes to screening of electrostatic repulsions, SDS micelles do not contribute to screening. Thus, only a fraction of sodium counterions for SDS added above the CMC contribute to screening. The results indicate that attractive depletion forces induced by SDS micelles were not sufficient to compensate for the weakened ionic strength enhancement caused by SDS addition compared to NaCl. The ionic strength effects dominate the gelation process.

title: Polymeric Microsphere Fabrication for the Controlled Release of Therapeutics
abstract: Degradable polymeric microspheres (MS) were fabricated to encapsulate therapeutics, brimonidine tartrate (BT) and mesenchymal stem cell-conditioned media (MSC-CM), with an interest in the controlled release drug delivery for the treatment of glaucoma and chronic tympanic membrane (ear drum) perforations. MSC-CM MS and BT MS were fabricated using poly(lactic- co -glycolic acid) using single emulsion and double emulsion techniques with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) used as a surfactant. PVA from different lots and different vendors were used to try to determine their effect on MS degradation. Microspheres were suspended in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) and rotated in an incubator at 37°C, with drug release samples taken daily over the course of 2-4 weeks until the MS degraded. Spectrophotometric analysis, with a colorimetric assay used for the MSC-CM MS releasates, of the total protein concentration in the MSC-CM MS and BT MS releasates showed a stable plateau release preceded by a burst of drug release. Scratch assays were performed in vitro to determine the wound healing potential of human dermal keratinocytes that are in the presence of MSC-CM. ImageJ analysis of images of the scratches taken at 6, 12, and 24 hours indicated that the presence of MSC-CM caused an increase in wound closure.

title: Developing Small Organic Molecule Sensors from Single Stranded DNA Aptamers
abstract: By combining a biophysical model with a genetic algorithm, we computationally designed single stranded DNA (ssDNA) sensors for detecting small organic molecules of interest. These sensors have notable advantages over current methods of small molecule detection, being significantly less expensive than liquid or gas chromatography with mass spectrometry and have much higher throughput than enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. When bound by their ligand, the sensors undergo structural conformational changes that lead to cleavage activities that are readily detected by inline nanopore-based sequencing, such as the mobile Minion sequencing platform. These ssDNA sensors utilize aptamers, which are structured nucleic acids that bind to ligands of interest, for molecular recognition with high specificity. As a key novelty, multiple ssDNA sensors can be combined and multiplexed with each output distinguishable by unique barcoded nucleic acid sequences. We have successfully designed sensor sequences for tobramycin, 17-B-estradiol, and ATP to produce two-state behavior and ligand-activated sensors.

title: Confining Electrodeposition of Metals in Structured Electrolytes
abstract: The 2019 Chemistry Nobel Prize for Li-ion batteries substantiates the global importance of these devices in contemporary electronics. Even so, developing electrochemical systems with higher energy density than Li-ion batteries is critical for decarbonizing our society’s energy systems. One pathway towards improving Li-ion battery involves replacing the graphitic anode with Li metal. This change can increase the anodic energy capacity 10-fold and enables the use of high capacity, Li-free cathodes. However, Li metal batteries are inherently unstable because of the high reactivity of Li metal with organic electrolytes that results in the formation of a solid electrolyte interphase (SEI), an insulating layer on the Li anode surface. The SEI’s inherent inhomogeneity causes some regions on the anode surface to be more conductive than others. Thus, Li ions deposit unevenly on the metal anode, leading to the formation of sharp nucleates. Continual deposition due to the high local electric field at the tip of the nucleates forms ‘needle-like’ dendrites capable of piercing through the battery separator, causing short circuits and initiating thermal runaway reactions in organic electrolytes. These catastrophic processes can result in lethal battery fires. There have been several studies dedicated to the prevention of dendrite growth and thermal runaway reactions by means of a high modulus physical barrier. One notable study concluded that a modulus at least twice that of Li (~10 GPa ) is required to achieve stable, smooth electrodeposition. However, these high strength “solid-state electrolytes” (SSEs) have low ionic conductivity, which reduces the power these batteries can produce, and therefore limits their practical use. Thus, engineering techniques and materials to break this tradeoff are critical concerns. Recent theoretical studies have reported that rough dendrite morphology can be mediated using battery separators having pore-diameter lower than the critical (smallest) size of the dendritic nucleate. To evaluate this, we synthesized cross-linked polymer composite electrolytes with tunable pore size, which host organic liquid in these pores. We systemically varied pore size within our electrolyte systems and found that the materials are resilient towards dendritic growth below a critical pore size, as predicted by the theoretical studies. Further, by the housed organic liquid solvent within the polymer network, our electrolyte system could maintain ionic conductivity at room temperature. These results show that the tendency for battery failure by dendrite-induced short-circuits can be reduced in rationally designed electrolytes, opening the gateway for future work nanoporous electrolytes.

title: Evaluating the Sensitivity of the Momentum TM Magnetic Particle Imager for Ferucarbotran Iron Oxide Nanoparticles
abstract: Magnetic particle imaging (MPI) is a promising imaging technology that enables non-invasive quantitative visualization of the distribution of biocompatible superparamagnetic iron oxide (SPIO) tracers. MPI signal is proportional to SPIO mass, does not suffer from artifacts arising from tissue background signal, has no limitations in tissue depth penetration, and does not use ionizing radiation. These features make MPI ideal for characterizing in vivo nanoparticle biodistribution quantitatively. The objective of this study was to characterize the sensitivity of the new Momentum TM MPI imager (Magnetic Insight, Inc.) using the commercially available SPIO nanoparticle ferucarbotran. A serial dilution of ferucarbotran iron oxide particles was prepared with the iron mass determined using the 1,10-Phenanthroline colorimetric assay for iron quantification. All samples contained 1uL of solution and were measured in triplicate, in two different positions of the field of view. MPI scans were made using four imaging modes available in the Momentum: default, isotropic, high resolution and high sensitivity. Images were analyzed using VivoQuant to evaluate signal intensity in regions of interest containing the tracer samples. The limit of detection was calculated on the basis of analyzing the spontaneous background signal of empty scans and the maximum intensity signal of samples at low concentrations. It was found that ‘ high sensitivity’ scan mode (3 T/m) had a limit of detection ~38 ng Fe, whereas ‘high resolution’ scan mode (6 T/m) had a limit of detection of ~200 ng Fe. We also observed differences in signal shape and background across all different imaging modalities. Determining the MPI limit of detection and quantification of different SPIO tracers is important for the development of a variety of applications. Understanding the optimal magnetic characteristics of SPIO tracers and their behavior on the Momentum TM MPI will provide a better understanding of the capabilities of this instrument for particle characterization and biomedical application. This will ensure that reliable data can be obtained and understood. Future studies will include determining the limit of detection for in-house synthesized particles to understand the behavior and properties of particles in the MPI, facilitating optimization of tracers for MPI imaging.

title: Thiophene-Ethynylene-Based Viologen Derivatives: A Novel Platform of Photosensitizer for Photodynamic Antimicrobial Chemotherapy
abstract: Photodynamic antimicrobial chemotherapy (PACT) has an excellent efficacy on infections caused by bacteria, fungi, and especially resistant bacteria. Photosensitizers are an important impact factor in PACT. To address the lack of broad-spectrum property and relatively few alternatives of traditional photosensitizers, a novel thiophene-ethynylene-based viologen derivatives platform represented by 4,4'-(thiophene-2,5-diylbis(ethyne-2,1-diyl))bis(1-hexylpyridin-1-ium) bromide (TEHPB) is presented. TEHPB was synthesized via the reaction of 2,5-bis(pyridin-4-ylethynyl)thiophene and 1-bromohexane. As a quaternary ammonium compound, the cationic pyridine group enhances the hydrophilia of TEHPB. This study presents a new design to incorporate thiophene and ethynylene structure into viologens while preserving its conjugated system. Our study also provides a deeper understanding of structure-property relationships of viologen derivatives. We use the colony counting method to determine the phototoxicity and dark toxicity of TEHPB against the gram-negative bacteria Escherichia coli and the gram-positive bacteria Staphylococcus aureus by graphing the sterilization rate vs. concentration of TEHPB. The dark toxicity testing indicated that the minimum bactericidal concentration for E. coli was 0.98 μM, and the minimum bactericidal concentration for S. aureus was 1.95 μM. In the case that the light intensity of white light is 20 mW/cm 2 and the illumination time is 1 hour, the sterilization testing results show that with increasing concentration, TEHPB has a significant bactericidal effect. Herein, our experiments indicated that the minimum bactericidal concentration for E. coli was 0.25 μM, and the minimum bactericidal concentration for S. aureus was 0.125 μM. Because of its good antibacterial property against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, TEHPB has a great potential to be used as a novel broad-spectrum antimicrobial photosensitizer, and the platform of thiophene-ethynylene-based viologen derivatives may open a new avenue to develop and synthesize novel photosensitizer system.

title: Thermochromic Cholesteryl Liquid Crystals Characterization with Polarized Light Microscopy
abstract: Cholesteric liquid crystals have temperature responsive optical properties due to anisotropic molecular orientation that is dependent on temperature. Specifically, the twisted nematic phase creates a helical structure that reflects visible light; the pitch of the helical structure and the wavelength (i.e. color) of reflected light both depend on temperature. Such liquid crystals have applications for thermal mapping by cameras. This introduces a need to evaluate the behavior of liquid crystals through visual analysis. In this work, a method to determine the thermochromic properties of liquid crystals was developed by using polarized light microscopy (PLM). To examine the liquid crystals, rectangular capillary tubes were filled with different formulations, comprised of cholesteryl benzoate, cholesteryl pelargonate, and cholesteryl oleyl carbonate, of liquid crystals. The composition of the ternary mixture was varied to tune the thermochromic properties of the liquid crystal. The rectangular capillary tubes were sealed at one end, filled with liquid crystal; a thermocouple was introduced, and the capillary was sealed at the other end. After heating to approximately 50°C, the samples were imaged using polarized light microscopy as they cooled to ambient conditions. To observe the color change due to the change in the molecular orientation of the liquid crystals, imaging was performed at 10x magnification, the minimal field diaphragm, and about 50% aperture. To avoid saturation, images were captured with auto exposure, auto white balancing at 1 frame per second. The digital images in standard red, green, blend (sRGB) were transformed to L*a*b* color space Performing frame-by-frame analysis, observed changes in color were related to quantifiable changes in CIE L*a*b* values. Depending on the composition, the blue-start to red-end varied from of 23.0 to 25.4 °C, 25.3 to 30.3 °C, and 36.9 to 42.6 °C. Specifically, color transition temperatures between 23.0 and 42.6 °C were obtained by varying the fraction of cholesteryl pelargonate in the formulation. The analysis method developed was validated with UV reflectance; the color transition temperatures measured by PLM and UV were comparable. Interestingly, the polarized light microscopy method allows for more detailed characterization of color transition temperatures than achieved by UV spectroscopy.

title: Optimizing Lead Perovskite Formation in High Humidity
abstract: Perovskite solar cells (PSCs) have gained popularity recently due to their high efficiencies and low production costs. PSCs are often fabricated in a humidity controlled environment, because water degrades the perovskite layer. This project investigates the synthesis of PSCs in high humidity (>50%). In this study PSCs were synthesized using different perovskite and antisolvent combinations to achieve the best performance. The best outcome was achieved using a combination of 2.4% 1,3-Dimethyl-2-imidazolidinone (DMI). in the perovskite and diethyl ether as the antisolvent. This approach yielded an efficiency of approximately 4% (without a Hole transporting layer(HTL)).

title: Robust, Crosslinked Anion Exchange Membranes for Fuel Cell Applications
abstract: Fuel cell technology is a growing field of research and use due to potential applications in military, transportation, and space application. While internal combustion engines are less than 25% efficient at converting chemical energy into actual power, fuel cell technology can reach efficiencies up to 70%. In the last decade, research related to anion exchange membrane fuel cells has increased since these fuel cells allow non-noble metal catalysts, such as nickel, instead of expensive catalysts like platinum. Here, the goal is to develop stable membranes with adequate ion exchange capacity and conductivity as well as good mechanical strength and durability. A topdown approach using a commercially available cationic polymer creates an anion exchange membrane through crosslinking and casting. Further study on the anion exchange membranes includes measuring ion exchange capacity, water uptake, and rheological properties. By measuring the properties of membranes with different compositions and thicknesses, this research will advance the understanding of anion exchange membranes.

title: 3-D Printing of Energetic Materials
abstract: 3-D Printing of Energetic Materials Over the last decade 3-D printing has been at the forefront of materials processing. However, for energetic materials 3-D printing is in its infancy and many critical material parameters are unknown. In this work, we explore ceramic fuel based pyrotechnics, also known as pyrolants. For this study, a ceramic fuel (MgB2) and a fluoropolymer (THV) were formulated in five different ratios of 30/70, 40/60, 50/50, 60/40, and 70/30. The combustability, combustion velocities, density, thermal characteristics, and aging were all studied in the course of this project. All five ratios were printed as inks and 30/70, 50/50, and 70/30 were printed as filament for comparison. As the amount of MgB2 was increased, the combustion velocity increased significantly with the 30/70 ratio at 4.016 mm/s while the 70/30 ratio combusted at 35.197 mm/s. In addition to the combustion velocities, the density was also assessed. The printed inks had a density of 0.4-0.7 g/cc lower than the filament most likely due to the porosity from air pockets that occur during printing. This also explains why the ratio of 60/40 was lower than the 50/50 ratio, when it was expected to be higher. Using a Brookfield Rheometer, it was determined that the 60/40 ratio fell out of the expected range with an apparent viscosity of 2,000,000 cP higher than the other four samples. Over the course of eight weeks in an aging oven, the filament aged extremely well. There was no significant change in color or in burning rate leading to the conclusion that the printed pyrolant is reliable over time. Future studies should consider optimizing printing parameters to reduce porosity.

title: Diffusion and Mechanics of Styrenic Block Copolymer Organogel Formulations: An Overview
abstract: Block copolymer gels have gained significant interest as a useful material platform for numerous applications including drug delivery vehicles. Non-aqueous block copolymer gels, i.e. , organogels, offer advantages over their widely popular hydrogel counterparts including elimination of drying out due to solvents with negligible vapor pressure as well as the ability to create a hydrophobic environment for drug delivery. Here, we characterize the diffusion of model nanocarriers, swelling behavior, and mechanical profiles of various block copolymer organogel formulations. These gels are comprised of styrenic block copolymers, aliphatic oil, and a nanocarrier-forming surfactant, and are uniquely formulated to provide insight into the role different components play in gel properties. While mechanical properties are probed using standard quasi-static uniaxial testing, diffusion is quantified using a novel method that directly measures the retained nanocarrier mass in gels through FTIR spectroscopy. Absorbance measurements are taken at specific time intervals and a plot of retained mass versus time is generated. Utilization of this method allows the retained nanocarrier mass to be tracked even with changing pathlength and volumetric expansion, both of which result due to gel swelling. The current overview study indicates that the mechanical profiles and internal diffusion of block copolymer organogels are tunable through simple changes in formulation. In fact, the data suggests that the two gel properties can be altered independently.

title: The Effects of Sodium Dodecyl Sulfate Concentration, Salt Concentration, and of Types of Salt on Oil – in – Water Emulsion Stability
abstract: Emulsions are homogenous mixtures of two immiscible liquids where one phase is finely dispersed in the other. Emulsions are thermodynamically unstable and will ultimately separate 1 . Surfactants are often used to decrease interfacial tension between the two immiscible phases and extend the lifetime of the emulsion 2 . Emulsions are commonly found in consumer products. However, in the majority of consumer products there are a large number of additional ingredients used to give products certain properties. It is important to understand how different components such as surfactant concentration, salt concentration and ionic composition affects emulsion stability .

title: Hydrogen Peroxide Releasing Biomaterials for Vascularization in Bone Tissue Regeneration
abstract: In the United States, 5-10% of bone fractures result in nonunion. Traditional solutions such as autografts and allografts have significant side effects, including donor site morbidity and disease transmission, respectively. Although new regenerative engineering treatments have been developed, their high cost and limited scalability have prevented their widespread clinical adoption. An additional limitation of bone tissue regeneration is inherent tissue complexity as vascular and neural networks must be regenerated in addition to osteoblasts. The Biomodulatory Materials Engineering Laboratory is working to develop a cheaper and more widely applicable option for large volume bone repair using novel biomaterials. This project focuses specifically on using the simple signaling molecule hydrogen peroxide to induce the differentiation of endothelial cells from mesenchymal stem cells for bone tissue vascularization applications. First, the therapeutic window for the differentiation of mesenchymal stem cells into endothelial cells using hydrogen peroxide was determined by exposing the cells to various concentrations of hydrogen peroxide for one, three, and seven days. Proliferation and differentiation of the cells was determined for each timepoint using DNA/ATP assays and fluorescent microscopy, respectively. A novel hydrogen-peroxide-releasing biomaterial was then synthesized by modifying glutamic acid with hydrogen peroxide to form a peroxy acid (i.e., perglutamic acid). Future research will focus on leveraging perglutamic acid as a monomer for various degradable polymers (e.e, polyanhydrides, polyesters, polyamides), for which cell studies can be conducted guided by the already established therapeutic window. The effects of these new biomaterials on off-target cells will also be studied. After biomaterials for osteogenesis, angiogenesis, and neurogenesis have each been synthesized, they can be integrated for large volume bone repair through tissue regeneration.

title: Coal-Plastic Composites for Use in Construction Application
abstract: Wood-Plastic Composite (WPC) decking offers significant improvements to traditional treated lumber decking material such as increased weather resistance, durability, and easier maintenance. Despite superior quality, sales of WPC decking have been held back by its significantly higher price; a board of WPC costs more than three times the price of a traditional treated lumber board. Cost could be reduced by use of less expensive filler, by increasing the filler content, or by lowering the energy consumed to produce a board. In this study, coal is evaluated as an alternative to saw dust as a filler, due to its lower cost and potential to be used at higher filler contents. Novel Coal-Plastic Composites (CPCs) with coal contents up to 60wt% are characterized by testing if they meet certain building codes for decking applications at various filler contents and by comparing their traits to those of current commercially available WPCs. Some of the building requirements tested include mechanical strength, flammability, and service life. Research so far has yielded positive results: CPCs with 60wt% filler, the same filler content as most commercial WPCs, have been found to meet the building requirements. Further, some advantages over WPCs such as superior flammability properties and increased strength have been discovered, with comparable service life.

title: Fabrication of PbSe Quantum Dot Thin Films with an Inkjet Printer
abstract: The fundamental processes associated with the fabrication of epitaxially-connected quantum dot solids is neither well understood nor controlled. As a result, many of their anticipated acclaimed properties have remained elusive. Inkjet printing offers rigorous process control, enhances manufacturing scalability, enables film integration into a wide range of device platforms, and allows for patterned designs without further processing. PbSe quantum dot thin films are created at the interface of two immiscible solvents. The PbSe quantum dots are in the upper solvent phase, or superphase, and become epitaxially connected when a chemical trigger binds to the ligands on the facets of the quantum dots and removes them. Then, the chemical trigger-ligand complex enters the lower solvent phase, or subphase, promoting uniform thin film formation. For such a system to work in an inkjet printer, the subphase can be initially printed onto a wafer. Then, the superphase can be printed on top of the subphase. Finally, a chemical trigger can be applied and the film formation would occur. We optimized the jetting of the superphase onto a silicon wafer substrate. We varied the jetting conditions, such as the waveform, and the composition of the superphase, such as changing the concentration of PbSe or the solvent. We balanced the constraints due to the fluid mechanics and thermodynamics involved with droplet formation and uniform thin film formation. Our optimal superphase solution was a PbSe ortho-dichlorobenzene solution. In future studies, we will optimize jetting this superphase onto subphases and then initiate film formation.

title: Graphene Nanoscrolls Induced Unique Crystallization of Poly Lactic Acid
abstract: Poly (lactic acid) (PLA) has gained attention for its use in biomedical applications due to its biocompatibility and optical, mechanical, and barrier properties. However, it is usually found in an amorphous or semi-crystalline state, which causes it to be brittle and have poor toughness. In order to improve the mechanical properties of this polymer, extensive research has been put into effective ways to crystallize PLA. This is difficult as PLA crystallization is a slow process that does not comply with large scale crystallization measures. A way to counteract this problem is by incorporating a nucleating agent into the polymer to lower the activation energy needed to start crystallization and affect the shape of the crystals, thereby affecting the mechanical properties of the polymer. Graphene nanoscrolls (GNS) are rolled up sheets of carbon, created by overcoming an energy barrier of about 100s to 1000s J/mol applied to graphene nanoplatelets. Once this energy is added, the flat sheets roll up and do not unscroll due to π bond interactions between the carbon molecules in different layers keeping the structure strong. Graphene itself is known for its chemical functionalization capabilities and physical properties such as high mechanical strength and thermal conductivity. GNS contains these properties from its graphene source, but also differs from other carbon-based nanomaterials such as carbon nanotubes, as its unfused edged creates an open morphology. This unique shape allows for a lattice strain which can provide more mechanical strength and create new crystallization structures. In this study, graphene nanoscrolls were fabricated from graphene nanoplatelets and used in PLA crystallization to improve the mechanical and physical properties of PLA. This was done by sonicating a mixture of GNP and toluene for scrolling and then using liquid nitrogen for structural stability to create GNS. The GNS then dried at room temperature before being incorporated into a melt-mix crystallization with PLA. Different weight percentages of GNS to PLA were used to see the affect on crystallization. Samples were then characterized by SEM, TEM, FTIR, XRD, and underwent a nanoindentation test to determine how the crystal structure of PLA changed, if any chemical interactions occurred between the PLA and GNS, the crystal structure and changes in mechanical properties. Through these analyses it was determined that the addition of GNS to PLA increases the crystallinity, crystal structure, modulus and hardness without any chemical changes to the polymer.

title: Asymmetric Hybrid Solid Electrolyte with High Conductivity and Low Interfacial Resistance for Lithium Batteries
abstract: Asymmetric Hybrid Solid Electrolyte with High Conductivity and Low Interfacial Resistance for Lithium Batteries Zachary D Althouse † , Yubin He † , Haochen Yang † and Nian Liu *† † School of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA 30332-0100, USA Abstract Lithium-ion battery technology is already nearly ubiquitous in portable electronics and is increasingly being put forward as an option in electric vehicle applications. However, current Lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) possess intrinsic safety hazards because of their use of flammable organic liquid as the electrolyte. This makes solid state electrolytes (SSE) a very promising area of research as they lack the volatility concerns of their liquid counterparts. There are two main categories of solid electrolytes: polymer and ceramic. Polymer electrolytes have better interfacial contact and electrochemical stability, while being less mechanically strong. Ceramic electrolytes have good conductivity and mechanical stability but have poor interfacial contact. To mitigate the inherent weaknesses of each material, combining the two technologies into a hybrid electrolyte has recently been investigated. In this work, preliminary investigation into an asymmetric solid “sandwich” electrolyte has occurred. This design uses crosslinked polyethylene oxide (CPEG) and polycarbonate (CPC) SSE on either side of a ceramic electrolyte backbone (LLZO). Preliminary results have shown that the CPEG-SSE and UVPC-SSE exhibit high conductivity (0.36 mS/cm and 0.18 mS/cm, respectively) at room temperature. A high conductivity of 0.30 mS/cm was also observed for the asymmetric SSE (CPEG/LLZO/UVPC). The Li/CPEG/Li symmetric cell shows excellent cycling stability at 0.2 mA/cm 2 for 500 hours, demonstrating that CPEG SSE possesses good stability against Li metal anode. However, CV results suggest that CPEG-SSE has low anti-oxidation ability at higher voltage (>4 V vs Li + /Li). On the other hand, UVPC SSE showed an extended electrochemical window up to 4.6 V vs Li + /Li, but poor cycling stability in a Li/UVPC/Li symmetric cell. The Li-LiFePO 4 batteries with a symmetric SSE (CPEG/LLZO/CPEG) have demonstrated low interfacial resistance (<160 ohm) as well as excellent rate performance (155 mAh/g at 0.2 C, 93 mAh/g at 1 C, and 57 mAh/g at 1.5C). Further studies will be conducted to determine the electro-chemical stability and battery performance of the hybrid membrane. This design, if effective, could lead to increased development of a modular electrolyte system, in which specific polymers would be chosen based on the cell requirements and identity of the cathode and anode materials.

title: Eigencages: Learning a Latent Space of Porous Cage Molecules
abstract: Porous organic cage molecules harbor nanosized cavities that can selectively adsorb gas molecules, which lends them applications in separations and sensing. The geometry of the cavity strongly influences their adsorptive selectivity. For comparing cages and predicting their adsorption properties, we embed/encode a set of 74 porous organic cage molecules into a low-dimensional, latent “cage space” on the basis of their intrinsic porosity. We first computationally scan each cage to generate a three-dimensional (3D) image of its inherent pore cavity. Leveraging the singular value decomposition, in an unsupervised manner, we then learn across all cages an approximate, lower-dimensional subspace in which the 3D porosity images cluster together. The “eigencages” are the set of orthogonal, characteristic 3D porosity images that span this lower-dimensional subspace, ordered in terms of importance. A latent representation, or encoding, of each cage follows by approximately expressing it as a combination of the eigencages. We show that the learned encoding captures salient, inherent features of the cavities of porous cages molecules and is predictive of properties of the cages that arise from cavity shape. Our methods could be applied to learn latent representations of cavities within other classes of porous materials and of shapes of molecules in general.

title: Van Der Waals Adhesion Force for a Particle Interacting with a Rough Surface
abstract: The small gravitational forces characteristic in dust systems facilitate opposing dynamics: airborne suspension and adhesion to surfaces. To characterize the extent of particle adhesion, we investigate the van der Waals force between particles and rough surfaces using well-defined sinusoidal surfaces. Exact numerical solutions are carried out by creating an atomistic model and explicitly summing atom pair interactions between the particle and surface. In the case that the particle size is larger than the length scale for surface roughness, we derive an analytic model that incorporates force contributions from all asperities on the surface. Our analytic model accurately predicts the van der Waals force, in contrast to previous models which underestimate adhesion by not accounting for the effects of all surface asperities.

title: Development of an Environmentally Friendly, Biodegradable Temperature Sensor
abstract: Temperature sensors are a useful tool to monitor the temperature of an object. There are a few temperature sensors on the market that can be 3D-printed, but they are not biodegradable. There are also temperature sensors that are biodegradable but not used in additive manufacturing. The temperature sensor that will be developed in this experiment will possess both qualities. Biodegradable sensors are important for waste recyclability—being able to dispose of the sensor without harming the environment. The device is composed of D-Sorbitol because it is biodegradable due to its presence in plants during photosynthesis, which means it can be consumed naturally. The other major material used in the sensor that is environmentally friendly and biodegradable is cellulose nanofibrils (CNF). Electrodes for the sensor can be biodegradable, as well. 3D-printing—additive manufacturing—is useful when in mass production. By producing many devices in a batch or continuous process saves time, which in turn saves money for the manufacturing company. It makes this quality very valuable to potential in the market; therefore, the device could be integrated into a marketable product that can be used as a wireless, wearable temperature sensor. In order to achieve this goal, the voltage and temperature changes must be analyzed thoroughly, as well as an analysis of the materials being used. Finally, the materials must be able to be prove that additive manufacturing is a viable option for production. The purpose of this study is to determine how the voltage is produced when a temperature difference is applied and be able to predict the temperature of the heat source given the produced voltage.

title: Manganese Dioxide (MnO 2 ) Nanowire Phase Behavior in Various Polar Solvents
abstract: The focus of this work is to investigate the phase behavior of manganese dioxide (MnO 2 ) nanowires dispersed in various polar solvents. MnO 2 nanowires were synthesized using a facile double-solvent synthesis method. The resulting materials were characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and spectroscopy techniques. A range of MnO 2 concentrations was then dispersed in ethylene glycol, dimethyl sulfoxide, ethanol, and methanol. UV-vis spectroscopy was performed to determine the concentration of nanowires that could be dispersed in a supernatant and quantify dispersion stability in each solvent. Since the nanowires are anisotropic, they have the potential to form lyotropic liquid crystal phases with increasing concentration; such phases facilitate processing into highly aligned solid materials. However, poor nanowire-solvent interactions can result in the formation of isotropic flocs and aggregates which are detrimental to the manufacture of uniform materials. Therefore, optical microscopy, with and without cross-polarizers, was used to characterize the microstructure in each sample for alignment. These findings were compared to predictions based on Hansen Solubility Parameter calculations. These results will contribute to the overall field of nanowire liquid crystal research and will enable understanding of how the dispersion microstructure can be linked to potential applications in aligned films, sensors and energy storage devices.

title: Self-Assembly and Solution Structure of Supramolecular Bottlebrush Polymers
abstract: Supramolecular polymers are unique compared to traditional polymers in that they are composed of key reversible and directional secondary bonding. Secondary bonds, most notably hydrogen bonds, can be fine-tuned and can consequentially alter the polymer’s material properties. Studies on self-assembly of linear chains with sidechain pendants (approximating the structure of graft polymer) typically use short small molecules for hydrogen bonding, yet it is unclear how well short polymers (<5K Daltons) will assemble. To study the impact of how sidechain length impacts supramolecular assembly, hydroxyl terminated polystyrene (PSOH) side chains were blended on to a poly-4-vinyl pyridine (P4VP) backbone. P4VP was chosen as the backbone due to the strength of the pyridine groups as an H-bond acceptor while PSOH of varying molecular weights were used as the pendant chains. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) was primarily used to investigate the hydrogen bonding occurring in the blended samples. Employing FTIR methods provides fundamental results in analyzing the amount of the pyridine groups in P4VP that are participating in supramolecular self-assembly. Small angle neutron scattering (SANS) located at the NIST Center for Neutron Research (NCNR) was also used to track the mesoscopic solution structure. Final results from the FITR showed that a single hydrogen bond (OH-P4VP) appeared to be insufficient to drive self-assembly for even oligomeric polymer chains. These findings contrast from SANS results on a lauryl gallate (surfactant) polymer blends. These findings show promise in supramolecular graft polymer being based on the multiple hydrogen bonding sites.

title: Stability of Solid Oxide Fuel Cell Cathode Material Under Reducing Conditions
abstract: The performance and durability of solid oxide fuel cells (SOFC) are currently being held back by cathode materials. The cathode materials that this poster will take into question are LSCF, LSM, and different variations of PNO. LSM and LSCF are materials that are already being used as cathode materials and are being tested alongside the PNO to observe how they compare to one another. In terms of diffusion coefficients, lowest activation energy for oxygen reduction, surface exchange, and electrode polarization, PNO shows the highest potential for new SOFC. However, the instability of these materials can affect their long-term use and degradation over time. This poster will discuss the quantitative data of the materials’ phase transformation and degradation over time when exposed to extended periods of heating under reducing conditions. Cathode materials are being tested by being heated for upwards of 500 hours at 750°C, while x-ray diffraction analysis is completed at various intervals in order to gather phase data. This process is being completed under different reducing conditions, meaning the cathode samples will be heated in the presence of different gases: Nitrogen, Air, and Hydrogen. While under these conditions normal PNO can experience degradation, instability, and phase transformation. In order to stabilize the phase without changing the material, other compositions of PNO are being tested alongside the original.

title: An Open-Source Program to Simulate Time-Resolved Photoluminescence and Electron Transport in Semiconductors
abstract: Time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL) is a powerful tool to extract the material and optoelectronic properties of semiconductors. However, extracting relevant information from TRPL data can be challenging as many complex electron dynamics can exist in these materials. Therefore, simulating TRPL data as a function of various material properties is of interest to better understand these electron dynamics and correlate with measured data. Dedicated commercial software for simulating transient electron dynamics is, however, limited and cost-prohibitive. Here we introduce an open-source program that we have developed to simulate transient electron dynamics in semiconductors. This program uses numerical methods to solve non-linear coupled differential equations as these equations governing the transient diffusion, drift, and the decay of electrons – whose recombination is a precursor to photon emission – can generally not be solved analytically. Our Python application for generating, visualizing, and exporting electron dynamics and TRPL data will be shown. In addition, example TRPL simulations in comparison to experimental data will be shown for thin-film photovoltaic absorbers and semiconducting nanowires.

title: Optimizing Conditions for Thermal Exfoliation of Graphite Oxide Films
abstract: Thermal exfoliation of graphite oxide is an effective and economically feasible large-scale production method for graphene-based materials. These materials are desirable for various applications such as catalysts, selective membranes, semiconductors, batteries, and sensors. In the process of GO film synthesis, the vast graphene oxide (GO) theoretical monolayer specific surface area (2600 m 2 /g) is lost due the perfect face-to-face GO monolayer alignment. In GO synthesis, modified Hummers method was applied, and the GO suspension (2 mg/mL) was used to prepare drop-cast and wrinkled GO films of varying thicknesses. These GO films were thermally exfoliated in an instrument set low (10 K/min) and high (100<HR<1000 K/min) heating rates. At low heating rates, GO drop-cast films below thickness 36 µm exfoliated into low surface area (<37 m 2 /g) and non-porous reduced graphite oxide (rGO) films. GO drop-cast films with thickness above 36 µm subjected to low heating rates yielded rGO films with modest surface area (~171 m 2 /g). Independent of the film morphology (wrinkled/drop-cast) and thickness, at high instrument heating rates the graphite oxide films explosively exfoliated into rGO powder with fairly large surface area (~700m 2 /g) and total porosity (~1.8 cc/g). It seems there is a critical film thickness and heating rate at which mass (product gases) and heat generation rates surpass their transfer rates out of the rGO system and GO exfoliates explosively. Wrinkled GO films did not demonstrate significant differences in thermal exfoliation compared to the drop-cast GO films. These insights are valuable for researchers trying to optimize GO thermal exfoliation process to produce graphene-based materials in large scale for variety of application venues.

title: Improving Electrical Conductivity of Carbon Fiber By Metal Electrodeposition Method
abstract: Carbon fiber is a carbon-based material with the advantages of high surface area, high tensile strength, high chemical resistance, low density, and high stiffness along the fiber. These advantages build carbon fiber a very promising role as a substrate (e.g., an electron collector) in energy storage devices which can highly increase the gravimetric energy density. Therefor, carbon fiber could be the key component assembling a flexible energy storage device for wearable electronics. However, carbon fiber is not a very good electrical conductor and will increase the internal resistance and lower the output voltage compared with metal substrate and aluminum or copper electron collector. This work focuses on improving the electrical conductivity of Carbon Fiber Mat (CFM, 50mm × 20mm) by depositing a thin layer of pure metal on the surface. Several Metal/CFM composites were synthesized for this purpose. The best one shows an electrical conductivity one hundred times higher than that of the same size carbon fiber mat.

title: Synthesizing Silver Selenide Thin Films Via the Cation Exchange Process for Thermoelectric Applications.
abstract: Thermoelectric (TE) devices are unique semiconductor devices that can directly convert heat to electricity and vice versa to serve applications such as waste heat recovery and solid state cooling. Bismuth-Tellurium and other commonly used alloys have been shown to be high performance TE materials but are composed of elements that are toxic, rare and expensive to process. To accelerate the widespread adoption of TE devices, safe and abundant materials need to be integrated into TE devices at an economical cost. Prior research has involved synthesizing Ag 2 Se nanoparticles, however this is an energy-intensive and time consuming technique with poor yields. To tackle this problem, we optimize the TE performance of Ag 2 Se by producing it via a low-cost, solution-processable approach relying on the cation exchange of Cu 2-x Se to Ag 2 Se. Cation exchange has recently emerged as an extremely versatile tool that allows manufacturing of a variety of materials whilst maintaining the morphology of a known anionic structure. We report a maximum power factor (PF) of ~800 µWm −1 K −2 achieved via a simple thin film soak. This PF is the highest value reported to date for a solution-processable Ag 2 Se thin film at room temperature. This soaking technique allows for a safe, economical and scalable solution to using Ag 2 Se in a variety of TE applications.
